title: 01.2 · Random variables and distributions through problems
text:
9. Marginal and conditional densities

Worked example 17: marginal durations from the triangle
For a fixed total duration xx, the inspection time ranges from 0 to xx. Integrate along that vertical slice:
fX(x)=∫0x2dy=2x,0<x<1.f_X(x)=\int_0^x2\,dy=2x,\qquad 0<x<1.
For a fixed inspection time yy, completion must fall between yy and 1:
fY(y)=∫y12dx=2(1−y),0<y<1.f_Y(y)=\int_y^1 2\,dx=2(1-y),\qquad 0<y<1.
Both densities are zero elsewhere. Each integrates to 1. For example,
P(Y>1/2)=∫1/212(1−y)dy=14.P(Y>1/2)=\int_{1/2}^1 2(1-y)\,dy=\frac14.
In general the marginal densities are
fX(x)=∫−∞∞fX,Y(x,y)dy,fY(y)=∫−∞∞fX,Y(x,y)dx.f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy,\qquad
f_Y(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx.
The stated support determines where the integrand is nonzero and hence the effective bounds.


Worked example 18: inspection time for a given duration
In the same model, consider tasks with total duration close to x=0.8x=0.8. The allowable inspection times occupy 0<y<0.80<y<0.8, and the joint density is constant along the slice. Normalizing that slice gives density 1/0.81/0.8 on this interval. Therefore the model’s conditional probability of inspection before 0.2 is
P(Y<0.2∣X=0.8)=∫00.210.8dy=14.P(Y<0.2\mid X=0.8)=\int_0^{0.2}\frac1{0.8}\,dy=\frac14.
The general conditional density formula is
fY∣X(y∣x)=fX,Y(x,y)fX(x),fX(x)>0.f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)},\qquad f_X(x)>0.
For the triangular model it is 1/x1/x on 0<y<x0<y<x and zero otherwise. For each fixed 0<x<10<x<1, its integral over yy is 1. A conditional probability is found by integrating it over the requested range of yy.
Since XX has a density, P(X=0.8)=0P(X=0.8)=0. This formula is not the elementary event ratio with P(X=0.8)P(X=0.8) in the denominator. For this regular density model it describes the limiting distribution in increasingly narrow duration bands around 0.8. The supplement gives the precise qualification. If a duration is rounded or measured over a band, condition on that band instead.


Worked example 19: conditioning on a band
Suppose the maintenance report groups repairs by duration: we know only that a selected repair took between 36 and 48 minutes. The planner asks for the probability that its inspection occurred before minute 12. In the normalized variables of Example 16, this is P(Y<0.2∣0.6<X<0.8)P(Y<0.2\mid0.6<X<0.8). The condition describes a range of durations, rather than one exact duration.
The conditioning event has probability
P(0.6<X<0.8)=∫0.60.82xdx=0.82−0.62=0.28.P(0.6<X<0.8)=\int_{0.6}^{0.8}2x\,dx=0.8^2-0.6^2=0.28.
Throughout the band, x>0.6>0.2x>0.6>0.2, so every 0<y<0.20<y<0.2 lies inside the triangular support. The joint event has probability
P(Y<0.2,0.6<X<0.8)=∫0.60.8∫00.22dydx=0.08.P(Y<0.2,0.6<X<0.8)=\int_{0.6}^{0.8}\int_0^{0.2}2\,dy\,dx=0.08.
Their ratio is 0.08/0.28=2/70.08/0.28=2/7. This is an ordinary conditional-event calculation with a positive denominator. It answers a different question from conditioning on X=0.8X=0.8.


Worked example 20: continuous independence
The sensor-square model in Example 15 has fU(u)=1/2f_U(u)=1/2 and fV(v)=1/2f_V(v)=1/2 on (−1,1)(-1,1), and the joint density equals their product. These two errors are independent in the stipulated model.
For variables with a joint PDF, independence is equivalent to
fX,Y(x,y)=fX(x)fY(y)f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)
apart from sets of area zero. Is it true for the maintenance triangle? No: P(Y>X)=0P(Y>X)=0 under the joint model, while independent draws from the two marginals would allow such pairs. For example, on the rectangle 0.1<x<0.20.1<x<0.2, 0.8<y<0.90.8<y<0.9, the joint density is zero and both marginal densities are positive. The triangular support carries dependence even though the density is constant within it.

Question

Marginalizing does not mean assuming independence. Conditioning does not mean exchanging the two variables. A PDF value is not a point probability. A support restriction is part of the model, not an optional annotation.

title: 01.2 · Random variables and distributions through problems
text:
11. Independent exercises
State the sampling mechanism or density, the variable and the event in every answer. All application scenarios are hypothetical. These questions have no solutions in the student notes or supplement.

Discrete variables and the CDF
D1. Two fair dice. Roll independent fair red and blue dice. Let SS be their total. Construct the PMF, find P(S≥9)P(S\ge9), and find FS(7)F_S(7). Explain why totals are not equally likely.
D2. Financial loss records. Select one of ten loan IDs uniformly. Six have recorded loss ₹0, three have ₹300, and one has ₹1200. Construct the loss PMF and CDF. Find the probabilities of loss strictly greater than ₹300 and loss at least ₹300.
D3. Defects in a three-component kit. A quality engineer models the number KK of defective components in a kit containing three components. No independence assumption is supplied; the model specifies the count directly. Its proposed PMF is pK(k)=c(k+1)p_K(k)=c(k+1) for k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3, and zero otherwise. Find cc, P(K≥2)P(K\ge2) and FK(1.5)F_K(1.5).


Continuous variables
C1. Sensor error. Stipulate EE uniform on [−0.4,0.4][-0.4,0.4] volts. Give its PDF and CDF. Find P(|E|<0.1)P(|E|<0.1) and P(E=0.1)P(E=0.1).
C2. Soil moisture. An agronomist selects a location uniformly by area within a specified field and measures its soil moisture. Let ZZ be moisture expressed as a fraction of a fixed reference level. For this model all values lie between 0 and 1, and the induced distribution of moisture at the selected location has PDF fZ(z)=cz2f_Z(z)=cz^2 for 0<z<10<z<1, and zero otherwise. Find cc, the CDF, and P(Z>0.5)P(Z>0.5). This is a stipulated dimensionless model, not field data.
C3. Rounded latency. Use the latency PDF fT(t)=t/2f_T(t)=t/2 on [0,2][0,2]. A display rounds to the nearest 0.2 seconds. Find the probability of a displayed value 1.2 and compare it with P(T=1.2)P(T=1.2).


Joint, marginal and conditional PMFs
J1. Accounting issues. An accountant reviews whether each invoice has the required authorization and an attached receipt. These are separate checks: an invoice can fail either, both, or neither. Select one of the 20 reviewed invoice IDs uniformly. Let A=1A=1 mean missing approval and R=1R=1 mean missing receipt. The counts for (A,R)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)(A,R)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1) are 10,4,2,410,4,2,4. Construct the joint PMF and both marginals. Find P(A=1∣R=1)P(A=1\mid R=1) and P(R=1∣A=1)P(R=1\mid A=1). Are A,RA,R independent?
J2. Training outcomes. A training coordinator wants the overall assessment pass rate and the composition of the passing group. The assessment uses the same pass criterion for both tracks. Select a participant under a stipulated model: group 0 consists of participants on an introductory training track and group 1 those on an advanced track. The selection probabilities of the groups are 0.40.4 and 0.60.6. The conditional pass probabilities are 0.50.5 and 0.80.8. Construct the joint distribution of group and pass indicator. Find the overall pass probability and the probability of group 1 given a pass.
J3. Same marginals. Construct two different joint PMFs for binary A,BA,B with P(A=1)=0.3P(A=1)=0.3 and P(B=1)=0.6P(B=1)=0.6. Make P(A=1,B=1)=0P(A=1,B=1)=0 in one and P(A=1,B=1)=0.3P(A=1,B=1)=0.3 in the other. Find P(A=B)P(A=B) in each model. Explain what the marginals fail to tell you.


Joint and conditional densities
K1. Two processing stages. A job passes through two stages in sequence. Let XX and YY be the durations of the first and second stages, measured in hours. The total processing time is X+YX+Y. Stipulate a constant joint density on 0<x<20<x<2, 0<y<10<y<1, and zero elsewhere. Find the constant, both marginal densities, and P(X+Y<1)P(X+Y<1). Are the variables independent?
K2. Inspection before dispatch. A warehouse records the time XX when a package is inspected and the time YY when it is dispatched, both in hours after packing. Inspection precedes dispatch, and dispatch occurs within one hour. Stipulate a constant joint density on 0<x<y<10<x<y<1, and zero elsewhere. Find the constant, both marginals, fX∣Y(x∣y)f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y), and P(X<0.25∣Y=0.5)P(X<0.25\mid Y=0.5).
K3. A band condition. Use the maintenance model fX,Y(x,y)=2f_{X,Y}(x,y)=2 on 0<y<x<10<y<x<1. Find P(Y<0.25∣0.5<X<1)P(Y<0.25\mid0.5<X<1) by calculating two region probabilities. Explain why conditioning on X=0.8X=0.8 is a different question.

Appendix A · From ticket records to a probability triplet and a PMF
This worked example connects an outcome, a numerical recording, an event collection and a probability assignment using one small dataset. It is separate from the batch-inspection example in Section 1; its frequencies are different.

A.1. Begin with the question and the selection rule
An IT support team reviews ten closed tickets. A follow-up is an additional contact needed after the initial response. The team records the number of follow-ups for each ticket and asks: if we select one of these tickets uniformly, what is the probability that it required at least two follow-ups?
The following records are hypothetical. Selection is from this fixed collection, with each ticket ID equally likely; it is not selection from future tickets or from individual follow-up contacts.



Ticket ID
Follow-ups required




T1T_1
0


T2T_2
2

3


T6T_6

0

T10T_{10}
2



Five tickets meet the condition: T2,T4,T5,T7,T10T_2,T_4,T_5,T_7,T_{10}. Therefore the answer is 5/10=0.55/10=0.5. We now make explicit the probability model underlying this calculation.


A.2. The full probability model over ticket IDs
The outcome is the selected ticket ID, so
Ω={T1,T2,…,T10}.\Omega=\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_{10}\}.
Initially allow every subset of IDs to be an event. The power set 𝒫(Ω)\mathcal P(\Omega) is the collection of all these subsets, including the empty set and the full collection. It has 210=10242^{10}=1024 members. Define
Pfull(E)=|E|10,E⊆Ω.P_{\mathrm{full}}(E)=\frac{|E|}{10},\qquad E\subseteq\Omega.
Here |E||E| counts ticket IDs in EE. This is normalized counting probability: each singleton has probability Pfull({Ti})=1/10P_{\mathrm{full}}(\{T_i\})=1/10. The full triplet is
(Ω,𝒫(Ω),Pfull).\boxed{(\Omega,\mathcal P(\Omega),P_{\mathrm{full}}).}


A.3. A random variable records the follow-up count
Define
X:Ω→ℕ0,X(Ti)=number of follow-ups recorded for Ti,X:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb N_0,\qquad
X(T_i)=\text{number of follow-ups recorded for }T_i,
where ℕ0={0,1,2,…}\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}. For example,
X(T1)=0,X(T2)=2,X(T5)=3.X(T_1)=0,\qquad X(T_2)=2,\qquad X(T_5)=3.
The values occurring in these records are X(Ω)={0,1,2,3}X(\Omega)=\{0,1,2,3\}. The function takes a ticket ID as input and returns a count. Once an ID is selected, its recorded count is fixed; randomness enters through ticket selection.






NoteOutcome, observation and probability



T2T_2 is an outcome. X(T2)=2X(T_2)=2 is its numerical observation. The probability of selecting T2T_2 in the full model is 1/101/10. The probability of observing the count 2 will be larger because several tickets have that count.




A.4. Which events can the count distinguish?
Suppose a report reveals only XX, hiding the selected ID. Seeing X=2X=2 identifies a group of four tickets, but does not tell us which one was selected. The groups are the level sets of XX:
A0={ω:X(ω)=0}={T1,T8},A1={ω:X(ω)=1}={T3,T6,T9},A2={ω:X(ω)=2}={T2,T4,T7,T10},A3={ω:X(ω)=3}={T5}.\begin{aligned}
A_0&=\{\omega:X(\omega)=0\}=\{T_1,T_8\},\\
A_1&=\{\omega:X(\omega)=1\}=\{T_3,T_6,T_9\},\\
A_2&=\{\omega:X(\omega)=2\}=\{T_2,T_4,T_7,T_{10}\},\\
A_3&=\{\omega:X(\omega)=3\}=\{T_5\}.
\end{aligned}
We also write Ak=X−1({k})A_k=X^{-1}(\{k\}). This is an inverse image: collect all inputs that give the indicated output. It does not require XX to have an inverse function.
These four nonempty groups are disjoint and cover Ω\Omega. Any event decidable from the count must include or exclude each group as a whole. For example, “at most one follow-up” is A0∪A1A_0\cup A_1, and “at least two” is A2∪A3A_2\cup A_3.
The collection of all such events is
σ(X)={⋃k∈SAk:S⊆{0,1,2,3}}.\boxed{\sigma(X)=\left\{\bigcup_{k\in S}A_k:
S\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}\right\}.}
It has 24=162^4=16 members: choose independently whether to include each of the four groups. The empty choice gives ⌀\varnothing; choosing all four gives Ω\Omega. The groups AkA_k are called the atoms of this finite event collection because no smaller nonempty event in the collection splits one of them.






NoteWhy this collection is a sigma-algebra



A sigma-algebra contains Ω\Omega and is closed under complements and countable unions. Here a complement selects the remaining groups, and a union selects every group included by any constituent event. The result is always another union of the same four groups, even for a countable list of events. Thus σ(X)\sigma(X) satisfies all three requirements. Intersections are also available by taking complements and unions.
It is the smallest sigma-algebra making the count observable as a random variable. The full model can retain more information: σ(X)⊆𝒫(Ω)\sigma(X)\subseteq\mathcal P(\Omega), and equality is not required.


For instance, {T2}∉σ(X)\{T_2\}\notin\sigma(X) because it separates T2T_2 from the other tickets with count 2. In contrast, {T5}=A3\{T_5\}=A_3 belongs to σ(X)\sigma(X): in this particular dataset, count 3 identifies one ticket uniquely.


A.5. The triplet retaining only count-based events
Restrict the full probability assignment to these 16 events:
P(E)=|E|10,E∈σ(X).P(E)=\frac{|E|}{10},\qquad E\in\sigma(X).
The resulting probability triplet is
(Ω,σ(X),P).\boxed{(\Omega,\sigma(X),P).}
The sample space still consists of ten ticket IDs. What changes is which subsets are retained as measurable events. In particular,
P(A0)=0.2,P(A1)=0.3,P(A2)=0.4,P(A3)=0.1.P(A_0)=0.2,\qquad P(A_1)=0.3,\qquad
P(A_2)=0.4,\qquad P(A_3)=0.1.
For an event containing more than one group,
P(A0∪A1)=2+310=0.5.P(A_0\cup A_1)=\frac{2+3}{10}=0.5.
The Kolmogorov axioms hold: all event counts are nonnegative, P(Ω)=10/10=1P(\Omega)=10/10=1, and counts add over pairwise disjoint events. In a pairwise disjoint sequence of subsets of this finite space, only finitely many can be nonempty, so this also establishes countable additivity. In particular, P(⌀)=0P(\varnothing)=0.






NoteA restricted event collection does not make a ticket impossible



Pfull({T2})=1/10P_{\mathrm{full}}(\{T_2\})=1/10 is defined in the full model. The restricted measure PP does not assign a probability to {T2}\{T_2\} because that subset is outside its domain. This does not make T2T_2 impossible. It means the count-only model retains the group A2A_2, not every distinction within that group.




A.6. Read the PMF as probabilities of ticket events
The notation P(X=2)P(X=2) means the probability of the event consisting of all tickets with count 2:
P(X=2)=P({ω:X(ω)=2})=P(A2)=410=0.4.P(X=2)=P(\{\omega:X(\omega)=2\})
=P(A_2)=\frac4{10}=0.4.
The probability mass function is therefore
pX(k)=P(X=k)=|Ak|10,k=0,1,2,3,p_X(k)=P(X=k)=\frac{|A_k|}{10},\qquad k=0,1,2,3,
with zero mass at other values.

P(X≥2)=P(A2∪A3)=pX(2)+pX(3)=0.4+0.1=0.5.P(X\ge2)=P(A_2\cup A_3)=p_X(2)+p_X(3)=0.4+0.1=0.5.

title: 01.3 tutorial · From outcomes to joint distributions
text:
What this tutorial develops
Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu
Module 01 · Fundamentals of Probability and Random Signal Theory
Lecture 01.2 · Next: 01.4 meeting problem · Rigorous supplement
If the first of two coin tosses is heads, does that change the possible total number of heads? If a selected record belongs to a particular group, which denominator should we use? If diagnosis and repair times are related, does knowing one change the distribution of the other?
We answer these questions through three worked experiments: two coin tosses, selection from a smoking–cancer table, and continuous support-ticket durations. All counts and operational models are hypothetical or stipulated for teaching. The health table is not epidemiological evidence.
By the end, you should be able to identify the probability space, construct events from random-variable conditions, obtain joint and marginal distributions, normalize a conditional distribution, and test independence. We also calculate a closure-time probability for a function of two variables.
The recurring distinction is between a probability model on outcomes and the distribution of the values recorded from those outcomes. First map an outcome to values. To ask a probability question, choose a set of values and take its inverse image, the set of original outcomes producing those values. The probability measure acts on that event.
ω→(X,Y)(X(ω),Y(ω)),D→(X,Y)−1{ω:(X(ω),Y(ω))∈D}→P[0,1].
\omega\xrightarrow{(X,Y)}(X(\omega),Y(\omega)),\qquad
D\xrightarrow{(X,Y)^{-1}}\{\omega:(X(\omega),Y(\omega))\in D\}
\xrightarrow{P}[0,1].
Here an inverse image does not require an invertible function. Several outcomes may produce the same observed values.

1. Two independent fair coin tosses

Begin with the question
Toss a fair coin twice, independently, recording the results in order. We want to know how observing the first toss changes our uncertainty about the total number of heads. Fairness alone would not specify the relationship between the tosses; independence is an additional assumption.
An outcome is a complete ordered record, such as HT: first heads, then tails. The probability model is
Ω={HH,HT,TH,TT},ℱ=2Ω,P(A)=|A|4(A∈ℱ).\Omega=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\},\qquad\mathcal F=2^\Omega,
\qquad P(A)=\frac{|A|}{4}\quad(A\in\mathcal F).
Define XX as the total number of heads and YY as the indicator that the first toss is heads:
Y(ω)={1,first toss is heads,0,first toss is tails.Y(\omega)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{first toss is heads},\\0,&\text{first toss is tails}.\end{cases}

Joint distribution and its marginals
The joint PMF is pX,Y(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y)p_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y). It is nonnegative, and summing over all value pairs gives 1. Grouping outcomes by their recorded pair gives:

P(X=1)=P(X=1,Y=0)+P(X=1,Y=1)=14+14=12.P(X=1)=P(X=1,Y=0)+P(X=1,Y=1)=\frac14+\frac14=\frac12.
This gives the marginalization rule:
pX(x)=∑ypX,Y(x,y),pY(y)=∑xpX,Y(x,y).p_X(x)=\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y),\qquad p_Y(y)=\sum_x p_{X,Y}(x,y).
These are distributions of the recorded values, not replacement definitions of the original outcomes. Formally, the induced law of (X,Y)(X,Y) assigns a set DD of value pairs the probability
P(X,Y)(D)=P((X,Y)−1(D)).P_{(X,Y)}(D)=P\big((X,Y)^{-1}(D)\big).
A real random variable is a function whose threshold inverse images {ω:X(ω)≤t}\{\omega:X(\omega)\le t\} are events for every real tt. In these finite examples with the full power set, every real-valued function meets this requirement. For a pair, inverse images of Borel sets of value pairs must be events.


Condition on the first toss
If we are told Y=1Y=1, only HH and HT remain possible. Each has conditional probability 1/21/2. In particular,
P(X=2∣Y=1)=P(X=2,Y=1)P(Y=1)=1/41/2=12.P(X=2\mid Y=1)=\frac{P(X=2,Y=1)}{P(Y=1)}=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac12.
The conditional PMF is
pX∣Y(x∣y)=pX,Y(x,y)pY(y),pY(y)>0.p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)},\qquad p_Y(y)>0.

Independent tosses, dependent recordings
If XX and YY were independent, every joint cell would factor:
pX,Y(x,y)=pX(x)pY(y)for every (x,y).p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)\quad\text{for every }(x,y).
But two heads and a first tail cannot occur:
P(X=2,Y=0)=0,P(X=2)P(Y=0)=1412=18.P(X=2,Y=0)=0,\qquad P(X=2)P(Y=0)=\frac14\frac12=\frac18.
Thus XX and YY are dependent. The total XX includes information from the first toss, which YY also records. Independence of the two tosses does not imply independence of arbitrary functions that use overlapping information.
More generally, XX and YY are independent when
P(X∈B,Y∈C)=P(X∈B)P(Y∈C)P(X\in B,Y\in C)=P(X\in B)P(Y\in C)
for every pair of Borel sets B,CB,C. The PMF factorization is the discrete equivalent. One failed cell disproves independence; one successful cell does not establish it.
Open the two-coin demonstration. Select (X,Y)=(2,0)(X,Y)=(2,0) to see the counterexample. Then select (1,1)(1,1): that cell happens to factor even though the variables remain dependent. Compare with the two separate toss indicators, which are independent.
Practice check 1. Find the distribution of XX given Y=0Y=0. Identify its underlying outcomes before calculating.
Suggested stopping point. Ask learners to explain the difference between independent tosses and dependent recordings before moving on.

Specify the experiment before choosing a denominator

Ω={ω1,…,ω1000},ℱ=2Ω,P(A)=|A|1000.\Omega=\{\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{1000}\},\quad
\mathcal F=2^\Omega,\quad P(A)=\frac{|A|}{1000}.

What can these observations distinguish?
Knowing (S,C)(S,C) identifies one of four groups, not an individual within a group. Write
A11={S=1,C=1},A10={S=1,C=0},A01={S=0,C=1},A00={S=0,C=0}.A_{11}=\{S=1,C=1\},\quad A_{10}=\{S=1,C=0\},\quad
A_{01}=\{S=0,C=1\},\quad A_{00}=\{S=0,C=0\}.
The generated sigma-algebra σ(S,C)\sigma(S,C) consists of all unions of these four groups, including the empty union. A sigma-algebra contains Ω\Omega and is closed under complements and countable unions. Unions of the four groups satisfy these conditions: complementation selects the remaining groups, and any union still selects groups.
All four groups are nonempty, so they are the four atoms of this observation-based collection and |σ(S,C)|=24=16|\sigma(S,C)|=2^4=16. This is much smaller than |2Ω|=21000|2^\Omega|=2^{1000}. For example, the event {C=1}=A11∪A01\{C=1\}=A_{11}\cup A_{01} is available from the observations, but a singleton individual ID is not. This is information lost by recording only the two attributes, not a claim that an individual has probability zero in the original model.


Conditional questions and Bayes’ theorem
Among smoker-labelled records, 60 of 300 have a cancer diagnosis:
P(C=1∣S=1)=60300=0.060.30=0.20.P(C=1\mid S=1)=\frac{60}{300}=\frac{0.06}{0.30}=0.20.
Among records with a cancer diagnosis, 60 of 95 have the smoker label:
P(S=1∣C=1)=6095=0.060.095≈0.632.P(S=1\mid C=1)=\frac{60}{95}=\frac{0.06}{0.095}\approx0.632.
The same numerator is divided by different conditioning-group sizes. Reversing a conditional changes the question. Equating the two expressions for the joint probability gives Bayes’ theorem:
P(S=1∣C=1)=P(C=1∣S=1)P(S=1)P(C=1),P(C=1)>0.P(S=1\mid C=1)=\frac{P(C=1\mid S=1)P(S=1)}{P(C=1)},\qquad P(C=1)>0.
Here the denominator can also be recovered by total probability:
P(C=1)=0.20(0.30)+0.05(0.70)=0.095,P(C=1)=0.20(0.30)+0.05(0.70)=0.095,
because P(C=1∣S=0)=35/700=0.05P(C=1\mid S=0)=35/700=0.05. Substitution gives 0.20(0.30)/0.095=12/190.20(0.30)/0.095=12/19.
Since P(C=1∣S=1)=0.20≠0.095=P(C=1)P(C=1\mid S=1)=0.20\ne0.095=P(C=1), the variables are dependent under this fixed-record selection model. This calculation establishes an association in the invented table. It does not establish causation, estimate future risk, or justify generalizing to another population.

text:
3. Continuous diagnosis and repair times

Define what closure time includes
For one future support ticket, let XX be hours spent diagnosing the issue and YY hours implementing the fix. Assume these phases are sequential, with no waiting or additional work included, so the modelled closure time is T=X+YT=X+Y. These are assumptions for teaching, not measured service behavior.
A convenient underlying space is
Ω=[0,∞)2,ℱ=ℬ([0,∞)2).\Omega=[0,\infty)^2,\qquad\mathcal F=\mathcal B([0,\infty)^2).
An outcome ω=(x,y)\omega=(x,y) is a complete pair of phase durations. The variables are coordinate projections: X(x,y)=xX(x,y)=x, Y(x,y)=yY(x,y)=y. We specify PP using a density:
P(A)=∬AfX,Y(x,y)dxdy,A∈ℱ.P(A)=\iint_A f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy,\qquad A\in\mathcal F.
The support of the density will be a rectangle or a triangle inside this space. Outside that support the model assigns probability zero. The identity representation is convenient, but the underlying outcome and the recorded values remain conceptually different objects.


Rectangle model: calculate a region probability
Stipulate that (X,Y)(X,Y) is uniform over 0≤x≤20\le x\le2, 0≤y≤30\le y\le3. What is the chance that diagnosis takes at most one hour and repair at most 1.5 hours?
The full rectangle has area 6 square hours; the qualifying rectangle has area 1×1.5=1.51\times1.5=1.5. Uniform weighting gives probability 1.5/6=1/41.5/6=1/4.
The joint density is consequently
fX,Y(x,y)={1/6,0≤x≤2,0≤y≤3,0,otherwise.f_{X,Y}(x,y)=\begin{cases}1/6,&0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
A joint PDF is nonnegative and integrates to 1 over the plane. Its integral over a region is the probability that the recorded pair belongs to that region. Here
∫02∫0316dydx=1,P(X≤1,Y≤1.5)=∫01∫01.516dydx=14.\int_0^2\int_0^3\frac16\,dy\,dx=1,\qquad
P(X\le1,Y\le1.5)=\int_0^1\int_0^{1.5}\frac16\,dy\,dx=\frac14.
A density value is not a point probability: P(X=x,Y=y)=0P(X=x,Y=y)=0 for each point in this model. The density has units of inverse square hours; integration over area produces a dimensionless probability.
For either discrete or continuous variables, the joint CDF is
FX,Y(a,b)=P(X≤a,Y≤b).F_{X,Y}(a,b)=P(X\le a,Y\le b).
It accumulates probability over a lower-left region. The calculation above is FX,Y(1,1.5)F_{X,Y}(1,1.5); a CDF value is a probability, whereas a PDF value is a density.


Marginals: retain one duration
To find P(X≤1)P(X\le1) regardless of repair time, include all 0≤y≤30\le y\le3:
P(X≤1)=∫01∫0316dydx=12.P(X\le1)=\int_0^1\int_0^3\frac16\,dy\,dx=\frac12.
The inner integral gives the marginal density of XX. In general,
fX(x)=∫−∞∞fX,Y(x,y)dy,fY(y)=∫−∞∞fX,Y(x,y)dx.f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy,\qquad
f_Y(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx.
For this rectangle,
fX(x)=12(0≤x≤2),fY(y)=13(0≤y≤3),f_X(x)=\frac12\quad(0\le x\le2),\qquad
f_Y(y)=\frac13\quad(0\le y\le3),
with both densities zero outside their stated intervals. Integrating over the other variable plays the same role as summing over the other column or row in a joint PMF.


Conditional density and independence
First condition on a band with positive probability. Among outcomes with 0.5<X<10.5<X<1, the proportion with Y≤1Y\le1 is
P(Y≤1∣0.5<X<1)=(0.5)(1)/6(0.5)(3)/6=13.P(Y\le1\mid0.5<X<1)=\frac{(0.5)(1)/6}{(0.5)(3)/6}=\frac13.
The factor corresponding to the diagnosis band cancels. This suggests that knowing diagnosis time does not change the repair distribution in this particular model.
For a jointly distributed pair admitting a PDF, a conditional-density version is
fY∣X(y∣x)=fX,Y(x,y)fX(x),0<fX(x)<∞.f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)},\qquad0<f_X(x)<\infty.
It integrates to 1 in yy for almost every such xx. This is not the elementary event ratio with denominator P(X=x)P(X=x), which is zero here. The density ratio supplies a conditional distribution; the supplement explains its narrow-band interpretation and why values on null conditioning sets are not uniquely prescribed.
For 0<x<20<x<2, the natural formula gives fY∣X(y∣x)=1/3f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=1/3 on [0,3][0,3], zero elsewhere. It does not change with xx. Moreover,
fX,Y(x,y)=fX(x)fY(y)f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)
almost everywhere on the entire plane, including where the densities vanish. This factorization is equivalent to independence when a joint PDF exists. Thus XX and YY are independent under the stipulated rectangle model.

4. Change the support: dependent continuous durations

A triangular operational model
Now replace the rectangle assumption by 0≤Y≤X≤20\le Y\le X\le2: repair never lasts longer than diagnosis in this hypothetical model. Stipulate uniform density on that triangle. Its area is 22, so
fX,Y(x,y)={1/2,0≤y≤x≤2,0,otherwise.f_{X,Y}(x,y)=\begin{cases}1/2,&0\le y\le x\le2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
The total probability is ∫02∫0x(1/2)dydx=∫02x/2dx=1\int_0^2\int_0^x(1/2)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^2 x/2\,dx=1. A constant density on a triangle does not imply independence: the allowable repair interval depends on diagnosis time.
For instance, if diagnosis takes at most one hour, repair cannot exceed one hour. Hence
P(X≤1,Y>1)=0.P(X\le1,Y>1)=0.
We now calculate the marginals to compare this joint probability with their product.


Work through the limits of integration
At a fixed x∈[0,2]x\in[0,2], allowable yy runs from 0 to xx. At a fixed y∈[0,2]y\in[0,2], allowable xx runs from yy to 2. Therefore
fX(x)=∫0x12dy=x2,fY(y)=∫y212dx=2−y2,f_X(x)=\int_0^x\frac12\,dy=\frac{x}{2},\qquad
f_Y(y)=\int_y^2\frac12\,dx=\frac{2-y}{2},
on [0,2][0,2], with zero values outside. Both integrate to 1. In particular,
P(X≤1)=∫01x2dx=14,P(Y>1)=∫122−y2dy=14.P(X\le1)=\int_0^1\frac{x}{2}\,dx=\frac14,\qquad
P(Y>1)=\int_1^2\frac{2-y}{2}\,dy=\frac14.
Their product is 1/161/16, different from the joint probability 0. This proves dependence using events with positive marginal probabilities, without relying on density values at a single point.


Conditioning changes the distribution
For 0<x<20<x<2, divide by the marginal density:
fY∣X(y∣x)={1/x,0≤y≤x,0,otherwise.f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\begin{cases}1/x,&0\le y\le x,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
The natural conditional distribution is uniform on [0,x][0,x], whose length changes with xx. It is normalized because ∫0x(1/x)dy=1\int_0^x(1/x)\,dy=1. For example,
P(Y≤0.5∣X=1)=∫00.51dy=12,P(Y\le0.5\mid X=1)=\int_0^{0.5}1\,dy=\frac12,
whereas
P(Y≤0.5∣X=1.5)=∫00.511.5dy=13.P(Y\le0.5\mid X=1.5)=\int_0^{0.5}\frac1{1.5}\,dy=\frac13.
These use the stated conditional-density version, not ratios of point-event probabilities. At x=0x=0, the marginal density is zero and the ratio is undefined.
Open the continuous-support demonstration. Switch between rectangle and triangle, then move the diagnosis-time slider. Compare the conditional repair density with its marginal density, and compare the joint-event probability with the product of marginals.


Transform the pair: closure within two hours
A service manager asks for the probability of modelled closure within two hours. The new random variable is T(ω)=X(ω)+Y(ω)T(\omega)=X(\omega)+Y(\omega). Its threshold event is
{T≤2}={(x,y):0≤y≤x≤2,x+y≤2}.\{T\le2\}=\{(x,y):0\le y\le x\le2,\ x+y\le2\}.
For 0≤x≤10\le x\le1, the upper limit on yy is xx; for 1<x≤21<x\le2, it is 2−x2-x. Thus
P(T≤2)=∫01∫0x12dydx+∫12∫02−x12dydx=14+14=12.\begin{aligned}
P(T\le2)
&=\int_0^1\int_0^x\frac12\,dy\,dx
+\int_1^2\int_0^{2-x}\frac12\,dy\,dx\\
&=\frac14+\frac14=\frac12.
\end{aligned}
This computes one CDF value FT(2)F_T(2) by finding an inverse-image region. It does not require deriving the whole density of TT, and it does not validate the stipulated duration model for a real service.
Practice check 3. In the triangle model, find P(Y≤0.5)P(Y\le0.5) and compare it with P(Y≤0.5∣X=1)P(Y\le0.5\mid X=1). Draw or describe both regions or slices first.
Practice check 4. In the rectangle model, identify the region X+Y≤2X+Y\le2 and calculate its probability. Explain which model assumption changes the result relative to the triangle.

title: 01.4 worked example · Two friends who may not meet
text:
1. The question and the experiment
Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu
Module 01 · Fundamentals of Probability and Random Signal Theory
Previous: 01.3 worked tutorial · Next: 01.5 expectation · Distribution-theory supplement
Appendix A: complete waiting-time CDF, mixed law, mean and variance · CDF and density sliders
Two friends agree to meet at a reference time t=0t=0. Each arrives during the following hour. Whoever arrives first waits for 15 minutes, then leaves if the other has not arrived. What is the probability that they do not meet?
This student-raised problem lets us distinguish a set of outcomes from the probability assigned to it. We will solve the same question under two stipulated arrival models: independent uniform arrivals, and independent arrivals with a density that decreases over the hour. Neither is claimed to describe observed arrival behavior.
We assume each friend does arrive within the hour, the first arrival waits the full 15 minutes even if that extends beyond the hour, and arrival exactly at the departure time counts as a meeting. The boundary convention does not affect probabilities under the two density models below.

title: 01.4 worked example · Two friends who may not meet
text:
Identify the probability objects
Measure time in hours. An outcome is the ordered pair ω=(tA,tB)\omega=(t_A,t_B): A’s arrival time first, B’s second. For example, (0.2,0.3)(0.2,0.3) means A arrives after 12 minutes and B after 18 minutes; they meet because the gap is six minutes.
Take
Ω=[0,1]2,ℱ=ℬ([0,1]2).\Omega=[0,1]^2,\qquad \mathcal F=\mathcal B([0,1]^2).
The Borel sigma-algebra includes the rectangles, triangles and diagonal bands used here. Define the coordinate random variables
TA(tA,tB)=tA,TB(tA,tB)=tB.T_A(t_A,t_B)=t_A,\qquad T_B(t_A,t_B)=t_B.
The triplet is (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), but the specification is incomplete until we choose PP. A joint density will assign probabilities to events by integration.

section: 2. Describe the event before choosing a density
text:
2. Describe the event before choosing a density
The waiting allowance is δ=15/60=1/4\delta=15/60=1/4 hour. The friends meet precisely when their arrival-time difference is at most δ\delta:
Mδ={ω:|TA(ω)−TB(ω)|≤δ}.M_\delta=\{\omega:|T_A(\omega)-T_B(\omega)|\le\delta\}.
Its complement, the event asked for, is
Nδ={ω:|TA(ω)−TB(ω)|>δ}.N_\delta=\{\omega:|T_A(\omega)-T_B(\omega)|>\delta\}.
Split the no-meeting event into two disjoint possibilities:
Nδ={TB>TA+δ}∪{TA>TB+δ}.N_\delta=\{T_B>T_A+\delta\}\ \cup\ \{T_A>T_B+\delta\}.
In the first, B arrives too late for A; in the second, A arrives too late for B. On the unit square with tAt_A horizontal and tBt_B vertical, the meeting event is the band between tB=tA−δt_B=t_A-\delta and tB=tA+δt_B=t_A+\delta. The two remaining corner triangles form NδN_\delta. These are measurable regions, so PP can act on them.
Before calculating: sketch the unit square and locate (0.2,0.3)(0.2,0.3) and (0.1,0.8)(0.1,0.8). Decide which belongs to the meeting band. The model has not yet told us whether area alone gives probability.
Open the waiting-time demonstration. Both panels use the same square and meeting band. Their background shading represents different joint densities.

title: 01.4 worked example · Two friends who may not meet
text:
3. Model U: independent uniform arrivals

Specify the measure
Assume TAT_A and TBT_B are independent and each uniform on [0,1][0,1]. Their marginal densities are 1 on that interval, zero elsewhere. Independence gives
fU(tA,tB)={1,(tA,tB)∈[0,1]2,0,otherwise.f_U(t_A,t_B)=\begin{cases}1,&(t_A,t_B)\in[0,1]^2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
For a Borel event E⊆ΩE\subseteq\Omega,
PU(E)=∬E1dtAdtB.P_U(E)=\iint_E1\,dt_A\,dt_B.
This integrates to 1 on the square. Under this particular measure, probability equals area. Merely specifying the square would not justify equal area weights.


Geometry first: probability of not meeting
At δ=1/4\delta=1/4, each no-meeting triangle has two perpendicular sides of length 1−δ=3/41-\delta=3/4. Its area is
12(34)2=932.\frac12\left(\frac34\right)^2=\frac9{32}.
The triangles are disjoint, so
PU(N1/4)=2(932)=916=0.5625.P_U(N_{1/4})=2\left(\frac9{32}\right)=\boxed{\frac9{16}=0.5625}.
Consequently,
PU(M1/4)=1−916=716=0.4375.P_U(M_{1/4})=1-\frac9{16}=\boxed{\frac7{16}=0.4375}.
The answer to the original no-meeting question is 56.25% under independent uniform arrivals.


Recover the result by a double integral
For the upper triangle, 0≤tA<3/40\le t_A<3/4 and tA+1/4<tB≤1t_A+1/4<t_B\le1. Symmetry of this joint density under exchanging the friends gives equal probabilities to the two triangles:
PU(N1/4)=2∫03/4∫tA+1/411dtBdtA=2∫03/4(34−tA)dtA=2[34tA−tA22]03/4=916.\begin{aligned}
P_U(N_{1/4})
&=2\int_0^{3/4}\int_{t_A+1/4}^1 1\,dt_B\,dt_A\\
&=2\int_0^{3/4}\left(\frac34-t_A\right)dt_A\\
&=2\left[\frac34t_A-\frac{t_A^2}{2}\right]_0^{3/4}
=\frac9{16}.
\end{aligned}
Integration adds density over the original event, just as a finite probability model adds outcome weights. The factor of 2 uses symmetry; independence alone would not justify it if the two arrival distributions differed.
Suggested stopping point. Have learners explain the integration bounds and why the two triangles have equal probabilities before changing the arrival model.

section: 4. Model E: independent arrivals weighted toward earlier times
text:
4. Model E: independent arrivals weighted toward earlier times

Normalize the proposed marginal density
Keep the same experiment and waiting rule. Now stipulate that each arrival has density proportional to 1−t1-t on [0,1][0,1]. With fT(t)=c(1−t)f_T(t)=c(1-t) there,
1=∫01c(1−t)dt=c[t−t22]01=c2,1=\int_0^1c(1-t)\,dt=c\left[t-\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\frac c2,
so
fT(t)={2(1−t),0≤t≤1,0,otherwise.f_T(t)=\begin{cases}2(1-t),&0\le t\le1,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
This is a different hypothetical model, not a conclusion that these friends actually arrive early. A higher density near zero means an interval of fixed small length near zero receives more probability than one near the end of the hour. A single exact time still has probability zero.
For example,
PE(TA≤1/4)=∫01/42(1−t)dt=[2t−t2]01/4=716,P_E(T_A\le1/4)=\int_0^{1/4}2(1-t)\,dt
=\left[2t-t^2\right]_0^{1/4}=\frac7{16},
compared with 1/41/4 in Model U.


Independence still holds, but the measure changes
Assume the two arrivals are independent with this same marginal density. The joint density is
fE(tA,tB)=4(1−tA)(1−tB)on [0,1]2,f_E(t_A,t_B)=4(1-t_A)(1-t_B)\quad\text{on }[0,1]^2,
and zero elsewhere. It integrates to 1 because each marginal integrates to 1. The probability measure is now
PE(E)=∬E4(1−tA)(1−tB)dtAdtB.P_E(E)=\iint_E4(1-t_A)(1-t_B)\,dt_A\,dt_B.
The outcome space, sigma-algebra, coordinate functions and meeting event are unchanged. Only the probability measure changes. Probability is no longer the unweighted area of a region.


Integrate over the same two triangles
The density remains symmetric in tA,tBt_A,t_B. Hence
PE(N1/4)=2∫03/4∫tA+1/414(1−tA)(1−tB)dtBdtA.P_E(N_{1/4})=2\int_0^{3/4}\int_{t_A+1/4}^1
4(1-t_A)(1-t_B)\,dt_B\,dt_A.
For a fixed tAt_A,
∫tA+1/41(1−tB)dtB=12(34−tA)2.\int_{t_A+1/4}^1(1-t_B)\,dt_B
=\frac12\left(\frac34-t_A\right)^2.
Thus
PE(N1/4)=4∫03/4(1−tA)(34−tA)2dtA.P_E(N_{1/4})=4\int_0^{3/4}(1-t_A)\left(\frac34-t_A\right)^2dt_A.
To show the remaining arithmetic, put u=3/4−tAu=3/4-t_A, so 1−tA=1/4+u1-t_A=1/4+u:
PE(N1/4)=4∫03/4(14+u)u2du=4[u312+u44]03/4=964+81256=117256≈0.45703125.\begin{aligned}
P_E(N_{1/4})
&=4\int_0^{3/4}\left(\frac14+u\right)u^2\,du\\
&=4\left[\frac{u^3}{12}+\frac{u^4}{4}\right]_0^{3/4}\\
&=\frac9{64}+\frac{81}{256}
=\boxed{\frac{117}{256}\approx0.45703125}.
\end{aligned}
Therefore
PE(M1/4)=1−117256=139256≈0.54296875.P_E(M_{1/4})=1-\frac{117}{256}=\boxed{\frac{139}{256}\approx0.54296875}.








Arrival model
Meet within the waiting allowance
Do not meet




Independent uniform
7/16=43.75%7/16=43.75\%
9/16=56.25%9/16=56.25\%


Independent decreasing-density
139/256≈54.30%139/256\approx54.30\%
117/256≈45.70%117/256\approx45.70\%



Both models assume independent arrivals. In this comparison, changing both marginal densities increases the probability that the two times are close. Independence does not fix the meeting probability. Nor does the calculation prove that every possible model favoring early arrivals must improve it.

section: 5. Transform the pair into an arrival-time gap
text:
5. Transform the pair into an arrival-time gap

A one-dimensional variable for the same question
Define the measurable function g(tA,tB)=|tA−tB|g(t_A,t_B)=|t_A-t_B| and the random variable
D=g(TA,TB)=|TA−TB|.D=g(T_A,T_B)=|T_A-T_B|.
Its values are gaps in hours, from 0 to 1. The meeting event is the inverse image
Mδ=D−1([0,δ])={D≤δ}.M_\delta=D^{-1}([0,\delta])=\{D\le\delta\}.
Many arrival pairs have the same gap. Thus the distribution of DD retains the gap information and discards the individual arrival times. It is induced by the original measure: for a Borel set BB of gaps, PD(B)=P(D−1(B))P_D(B)=P(D^{-1}(B)).


Derive the gap CDF and PDF under uniform arrivals
For 0≤d≤10\le d\le1, the two triangles outside the band of width dd have total area (1−d)2(1-d)^2. Hence the CDF, defined by FD,U(d)=PU(D≤d)F_{D,U}(d)=P_U(D\le d), is
FD,U(d)={0,d<0,1−(1−d)2=2d−d2,0≤d≤1,1,d>1.F_{D,U}(d)=\begin{cases}
0,&d<0,\\
1-(1-d)^2=2d-d^2,&0\le d\le1,\\
1,&d>1.
\end{cases}
Differentiating on (0,1)(0,1) gives a PDF:
fD,U(d)=2(1−d)(0<d<1),f_{D,U}(d)=2(1-d)\quad(0<d<1),
zero outside [0,1][0,1]. Its values at the endpoints do not affect any probability. It is nonnegative and integrates to 1. Recover the meeting probability:
PU(D≤1/4)=∫01/42(1−d)dd=[2d−d2]01/4=716.P_U(D\le1/4)=\int_0^{1/4}2(1-d)\,dd
=\left[2d-d^2\right]_0^{1/4}=\frac7{16}.
This density has the same formula as the individual arrival-time density in Model E, but it describes a different variable under a different probability measure. In Model E, the gap density is not 2(1−d)2(1-d).

section: 6. Vary the waiting policy, retaining the models
text:
6. Vary the waiting policy, retaining the models
Let ww be the waiting allowance in minutes and δ=w/60\delta=w/60. For 0≤δ≤10\le\delta\le1, the uniform calculation gives
PU(Nδ)=(1−δ)2,PU(Mδ)=2δ−δ2.P_U(N_\delta)=(1-\delta)^2,\qquad
P_U(M_\delta)=2\delta-\delta^2.
In Model E, the same integration with 1/41/4 replaced by δ\delta gives, with a=1−δa=1-\delta,
PE(Nδ)=4∫01−δ(1−t)(1−δ−t)2dt=4∫0a(δ+u)u2du=4δa33+a4=(1−δ)3(1+δ3).\begin{aligned}
P_E(N_\delta)
&=4\int_0^{1-\delta}(1-t)(1-\delta-t)^2\,dt\\
&=4\int_0^a(\delta+u)u^2\,du
=\frac{4\delta a^3}{3}+a^4\\
&=(1-\delta)^3\left(1+\frac\delta3\right).
\end{aligned}
Therefore
PE(Mδ)=1−(1−δ)3(1+δ3).P_E(M_\delta)=1-(1-\delta)^3\left(1+\frac\delta3\right).
At zero waiting time, meeting requires equal arrival times, a diagonal of probability zero under both models. At 60 minutes, all pairs qualify and the meeting probability is 1. Increasing the waiting allowance enlarges the event without changing either model’s measure.
Explore waiting times from 0 to 60 minutes. The demonstration evaluates these formulas exactly up to numerical rounding; its shaded grid is only a display of density, not a numerical probability estimator.
Practice check 1. If the waiting allowance rises from 15 to 30 minutes, does the meeting probability double? Calculate the result under each model and explain using the expanded band.
Practice check 2. Under uniform arrivals, what waiting allowance is needed for a meeting probability of at least 3/43/4? State your answer in minutes.
Practice check 3. Keep uniform marginal arrivals but suppose TB=TAT_B=T_A exactly. What is the meeting probability at zero waiting time? Explain which original assumption fails and why a two-dimensional joint PDF no longer describes this new model.

section: Appendix A · From joint arrivals to the actual waiting-time distribution
text:
Appendix A · From joint arrivals to the actual waiting-time distribution

A.1. Questions, assumptions and notation
If the friends arrive 40 minutes apart, the first friend waits only 15 minutes before leaving. The arrival gap and the actual waiting time therefore answer different questions. In this appendix we derive the distributions of both, then calculate the mean and variance of the actual wait.
The learning sequence is to construct the joint density, define a function of the pair, calculate its CDF from an event region, differentiate when a density exists, apply a second transformation, identify any resulting point mass, and calculate moments using the complete law.
We use Model U only: the two arrivals are independent and uniform during the hour following t=0t=0. Each friend does arrive within that hour. The first friend waits up to 15 minutes even if that extends beyond the end of the arrival window. Arrival exactly at the departure time counts as a meeting; this equality has probability zero in the stipulated model.
To remain consistent with the rest of this course, we write
D=|TA−TB|for the arrival gap,W=min⁡(D,1/4)for the actual wait.D=|T_A-T_B|\quad\text{for the arrival gap},\qquad
W=\min(D,1/4)\quad\text{for the actual wait}.
All formula arguments below are in hours, unless stated otherwise. WW records the wait of whichever friend arrives first, not the wait of a particular named friend or the sum of both friends’ waits. At a simultaneous arrival, define the wait as zero.
Open the interactive CDF, density and point-mass demonstration. Start at a 15-minute cap and compare the CDF immediately below the cap with its value at the cap. Then change the waiting policy.


A.2. Construct the probability triplet and joint law
An outcome is an ordered pair ω=(tA,tB)\omega=(t_A,t_B). The probability model is
Ω=[0,1]2,ℱ=ℬ([0,1]2),PU(E)=∬E1dtAdtB(E∈ℱ).\Omega=[0,1]^2,\qquad\mathcal F=\mathcal B([0,1]^2),\qquad
P_U(E)=\iint_E1\,dt_A\,dt_B\quad(E\in\mathcal F).
The coordinate variables TA(ω)=tAT_A(\omega)=t_A and TB(ω)=tBT_B(\omega)=t_B each have density 1 on [0,1][0,1], zero elsewhere. Independence gives
fTA,TB(tA,tB)={1,(tA,tB)∈[0,1]2,0,otherwise.f_{T_A,T_B}(t_A,t_B)=
\begin{cases}1,&(t_A,t_B)\in[0,1]^2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
Thus PU(E)=Area⁡(E)P_U(E)=\operatorname{Area}(E) for Borel regions in the square. Equal probability per unit area is a property of this measure; it does not follow merely from choosing a square sample space. Individual points have probability zero, so “uniform” means equal-length arrival intervals have equal probabilities, not positive equal probabilities assigned to individual arrival times.
An outcome is one pair; an event is a measurable set of pairs; a random variable maps each pair to a number. All subsequent transformations use this same probability triplet.


A.3. First transformation: the gap between arrival times
Define D(ω)=|TA(ω)−TB(ω)|D(\omega)=|T_A(\omega)-T_B(\omega)|. This is a measurable function with range [0,1][0,1]. It is deterministic given the arrivals, but random before the outcome is known.

For a real threshold dd, the CDF is FD(d)=PU(D≤d)F_D(d)=P_U(D\le d). When 0≤d≤10\le d\le1,
{D≤d}={|TA−TB|≤d}={−d≤TA−TB≤d}={TA−d≤TB≤TA+d}.\begin{aligned}
\{D\le d\}
&=\{|T_A-T_B|\le d\}\\
&=\{-d\le T_A-T_B\le d\}\\
&=\{T_A-d\le T_B\le T_A+d\}.
\end{aligned}
The inverse image of [0,d][0,d] is the diagonal band between tB=tA−dt_B=t_A-d and tB=tA+dt_B=t_A+d. Each excluded corner triangle has perpendicular sides of length 1−d1-d. Their total area is 2[12(1−d)2]=(1−d)22[\tfrac12(1-d)^2]=(1-d)^2. Therefore
FD(d)=1−(1−d)2=2d−d2(0≤d≤1).F_D(d)=1-(1-d)^2=2d-d^2\qquad(0\le d\le1).
The integration limits give the same result. For the upper excluded triangle, 0≤tA<1−d0\le t_A<1-d and tA+d<tB≤1t_A+d<t_B\le1:
PU(D>d)=2∫01−d∫tA+d11dtBdtA=2∫01−d(1−d−tA)dtA=2[(1−d)tA−tA22]01−d=(1−d)2.\begin{aligned}
P_U(D>d)
&=2\int_0^{1-d}\int_{t_A+d}^1 1\,dt_B\,dt_A\\
&=2\int_0^{1-d}(1-d-t_A)\,dt_A\\
&=2\left[(1-d)t_A-\frac{t_A^2}{2}\right]_0^{1-d}
=(1-d)^2.
\end{aligned}
The factor of 2 is justified by the symmetry of this joint law. Include thresholds outside the range to obtain
FD(d)={0,d<0,2d−d2,0≤d≤1,1,d>1.\boxed{F_D(d)=\begin{cases}
0,&d<0,\\
2d-d^2,&0\le d\le1,\\
1,&d>1.
\end{cases}}
This CDF is absolutely continuous. Its derivative gives a density, up to choices at endpoints:
fD(d)={2(1−d),0<d<1,0,otherwise.f_D(d)=\begin{cases}2(1-d),&0<d<1,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
Check normalization: ∫012(1−d)dd=[2d−d2]01=1\int_0^1 2(1-d)\,dd=[2d-d^2]_0^1=1. The gap is not uniform even though both inputs are uniform. Intervals of a given small length near zero receive more gap probability than intervals of that length near one hour. This statement compares intervals, not positive probabilities at individual points.
A CDF always exists for a real random variable. Differentiation recovers the full law as a PDF when the CDF is absolutely continuous; a continuous CDF alone is not a sufficient condition in complete generality.


A.4. Use the gap distribution to answer the meeting question
A 15-minute cap is 1/41/4 hour. The meeting event is M1/4={D≤1/4}M_{1/4}=\{D\le1/4\}. Consequently,
PU(M1/4)=FD(1/4)=2(14)−(14)2=12−116=716=43.75%.\begin{aligned}
P_U(M_{1/4})&=F_D(1/4)
=2\left(\frac14\right)-\left(\frac14\right)^2\\
&=\frac12-\frac1{16}=\boxed{\frac7{16}=43.75\%}.
\end{aligned}
The probability of no meeting is 1−7/16=9/161-7/16=9/16. This uses the distribution of the uncapped gap, not a distribution of actual waiting times.


A.5. Second transformation: cap the wait
The first arrival waits until the second arrives or the allowance expires:
W=min⁡(D,1/4)=min⁡(|TA−TB|,1/4).W=\min(D,1/4)=\min(|T_A-T_B|,1/4).

Equivalently,
W={D,0≤D<1/4,1/4,D≥1/4.W=\begin{cases}D,&0\le D<1/4,\\1/4,&D\ge1/4.\end{cases}
The composition (TA,TB)↦D↦W(T_A,T_B)\mapsto D\mapsto W changes the recorded quantity without changing the original probability measure. The range of WW is [0,1/4][0,1/4].


A.6. Derive the waiting-time CDF in three cases
Start from FW(w)=PU(W≤w)F_W(w)=P_U(W\le w).
Case 1: w<0w<0. A wait cannot be negative, so FW(w)=0F_W(w)=0.
Case 2: 0≤w<1/40\le w<1/4. Because the cap exceeds the threshold,
{min⁡(D,1/4)≤w}={D≤w}.\{\min(D,1/4)\le w\}=\{D\le w\}.
To check both directions: if D≤wD\le w, the minimum is at most ww; if D>wD>w, both DD and 1/41/4 exceed ww, so their minimum also exceeds ww. Hence
FW(w)=FD(w)=2w−w2.F_W(w)=F_D(w)=2w-w^2.
Case 3: w≥1/4w\ge1/4. Every possible wait is at most 1/41/4, so the event is all of Ω\Omega and FW(w)=1F_W(w)=1.
Combining the cases,
FW(w)={0,w<0,2w−w2,0≤w<1/4,1,w≥1/4.\boxed{F_W(w)=\begin{cases}
0,&w<0,\\
2w-w^2,&0\le w<1/4,\\
1,&w\ge1/4.
\end{cases}}
The middle interval excludes 1/41/4. At that threshold the event suddenly includes all the outcomes whose waits were capped.


A.7. Interpret the jump at 15 minutes
The left-hand limit and the value at the cap are
FW(1/4−)=716,FW(1/4)=1.F_W(1/4^-)=\frac7{16},\qquad F_W(1/4)=1.
For any CDF, a jump at aa has size P(W=a)=FW(a)−FW(a−)P(W=a)=F_W(a)-F_W(a^-). Here,
PU(W=1/4)=1−716=916.\boxed{P_U(W=1/4)=1-\frac7{16}=\frac9{16}.}
The transformation sends the whole set {D≥1/4}\{D\ge1/4\} to the one value 1/41/4. Although PU(D=1/4)=0P_U(D=1/4)=0, the larger event {D≥1/4}\{D\ge1/4\} has probability 9/169/16. A transformation can therefore create a point mass by mapping a positive-probability set onto a single value.
In the visualization, the open point at height 7/167/16 marks the left limit. The filled point at height 1 marks the CDF value at the cap. The vertical connector indicates the jump; it does not mean the function takes intermediate values at w=1/4w=1/4. The CDF is right-continuous.


A.8. Specify the complete mixed distribution
Differentiating below the cap gives the continuous component density
fW,ac(w)=2(1−w)𝟏(0,1/4)(w).f_{W,\mathrm{ac}}(w)=2(1-w)\,\mathbf1_{(0,1/4)}(w).
This is not a normalized PDF for the whole law:
∫01/42(1−w)dw=716.\int_0^{1/4}2(1-w)\,dw=\frac7{16}.
The remaining 9/169/16 is an atom at 1/41/4. For any Borel set B⊆ℝB\subseteq\mathbb R, a complete specification is
PU(W∈B)=∫B∩(0,1/4)2(1−w)dw+916𝟏{1/4∈B}.\boxed{P_U(W\in B)=\int_{B\cap(0,1/4)}2(1-w)\,dw
+\frac9{16}\mathbf1_{\{1/4\in B\}}.}
The integral and point mass sum to 7/16+9/16=17/16+9/16=1. Thus the law is mixed, with a continuous component and a discrete component. There is no ordinary density with respect to length that represents all its probability.
One may write the law as fW,ac(w)dw+(9/16)δ1/4(dw)f_{W,\mathrm{ac}}(w)\,dw+(9/16)\delta_{1/4}(dw), where δ1/4\delta_{1/4} is the unit point-mass measure at 1/41/4. This notation does not treat a Dirac mass as a finite-height PDF value. The visualization therefore shows the continuous density and the atom on separate, labelled scales.
Suggested stopping point. Ask students to explain why P(D=1/4)=0P(D=1/4)=0 and P(W=1/4)=9/16P(W=1/4)=9/16 can both hold before calculating moments.


A.9. Mean waiting time: include both components
Expectation is the probability-weighted mean. For the complete mixed law,
E[W]=∫01/4w2(1−w)dw+14916.E[W]=\int_0^{1/4}w\,2(1-w)\,dw+\frac14\frac9{16}.
The integral accounts for waits below 15 minutes; the second term accounts for the full-cap waits. Compute each contribution:
∫01/4w2(1−w)dw=2∫01/4(w−w2)dw=[w2−2w33]01/4=116−196=596,14916=964.\begin{aligned}
\int_0^{1/4}w\,2(1-w)\,dw
&=2\int_0^{1/4}(w-w^2)\,dw\\
&=\left[w^2-\frac{2w^3}{3}\right]_0^{1/4}
=\frac1{16}-\frac1{96}=\frac5{96},\\
\frac14\frac9{16}&=\frac9{64}.
\end{aligned}
Therefore
E[W]=596+964=10+27192=37192 hour.E[W]=\frac5{96}+\frac9{64}
=\frac{10+27}{192}=\boxed{\frac{37}{192}\text{ hour}}.
With Wm=60WW_m=60W in minutes, linearity gives
E[Wm]=6037192=11.5625 minutes.\boxed{E[W_m]=60\frac{37}{192}=11.5625\text{ minutes}.}
Under independent repetitions of the stated experiment, the sample average converges to this expectation. The result includes both successful and unsuccessful meetings; it is not the conditional mean among pairs who meet. It also differs from E[D]E[D], since a gap above 15 minutes is not fully spent waiting.


A.10. Second moment, variance and standard deviation
The variance is the expected squared deviation from the mean:
Var⁡(W)=E[(W−E[W])2]=E[W2]−(E[W])2.\operatorname{Var}(W)=E[(W-E[W])^2]=E[W^2]-(E[W])^2.
First calculate the second moment using both components:
E[W2]=∫01/4w22(1−w)dw+(14)2916=[2w33−w42]01/4+9256=196−1512+9256=16−3+541536=671536 hours2.\begin{aligned}
E[W^2]
&=\int_0^{1/4}w^2\,2(1-w)\,dw+\left(\frac14\right)^2\frac9{16}\\
&=\left[\frac{2w^3}{3}-\frac{w^4}{2}\right]_0^{1/4}+\frac9{256}\\
&=\frac1{96}-\frac1{512}+\frac9{256}\\
&=\frac{16-3+54}{1536}
=\boxed{\frac{67}{1536}\text{ hours}^2}.
\end{aligned}
Now subtract the square of the mean, using a common denominator:
Var⁡(W)=671536−(37192)2=1608−136936864=23936864 hours2≈0.00648329 hours2.\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(W)
&=\frac{67}{1536}-\left(\frac{37}{192}\right)^2\\
&=\frac{1608-1369}{36864}
=\boxed{\frac{239}{36864}\text{ hours}^2}
\approx0.00648329\text{ hours}^2.
\end{aligned}
Changing units multiplies variance by the square of the conversion factor:
Var⁡(Wm)=602Var⁡(W)=5975256=23.33984375 minutes2.\operatorname{Var}(W_m)=60^2\operatorname{Var}(W)
=\frac{5975}{256}=\boxed{23.33984375\text{ minutes}^2}.
The standard deviation returns to the original units:
SD⁡(Wm)=23.33984375≈4.831 minutes.\operatorname{SD}(W_m)=\sqrt{23.33984375}\approx\boxed{4.831\text{ minutes}}.
The second moment E[W2]E[W^2] and the variance are different quantities. Ignoring the point mass would give incorrect values for both the mean and the second moment.


A.11. Recalculate through survival probabilities
For a nonnegative random variable VV,
E[V]=∫0∞P(V>t)dt.E[V]=\int_0^\infty P(V>t)\,dt.
To see why, write each nonnegative value as its accumulated indicators: V(ω)=∫0∞𝟏{V(ω)>t}dtV(\omega)=\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{V(\omega)>t\}}dt. Interchange the two nonnegative integrals to obtain the formula. Likewise, V(ω)2=∫0∞2t𝟏{V(ω)>t}dtV(\omega)^2=\int_0^\infty2t\mathbf1_{\{V(\omega)>t\}}dt gives
E[V2]=2∫0∞tP(V>t)dt.E[V^2]=2\int_0^\infty tP(V>t)\,dt.
These identities apply to nonnegative continuous, discrete and mixed laws, with infinite expectations allowed. Here WW is bounded, so the moments are finite.
For 0≤t<1/40\le t<1/4, {W>t}={D>t}\{W>t\}=\{D>t\} and
PU(W>t)=1−FD(t)=(1−t)2.P_U(W>t)=1-F_D(t)=(1-t)^2.
For t≥1/4t\ge1/4, it is zero. Therefore
E[W]=∫01/4(1−t)2dt=[t−t2+t33]01/4=14−116+1192=37192,E[W2]=2∫01/4t(1−t)2dt=[t2−4t33+t42]01/4=116−148+1512=671536.\begin{aligned}
E[W]&=\int_0^{1/4}(1-t)^2dt\\
&=\left[t-t^2+\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^{1/4}
=\frac14-\frac1{16}+\frac1{192}=\frac{37}{192},\\
E[W^2]&=2\int_0^{1/4}t(1-t)^2dt\\
&=\left[t^2-\frac{4t^3}{3}+\frac{t^4}{2}\right]_0^{1/4}
=\frac1{16}-\frac1{48}+\frac1{512}=\frac{67}{1536}.
\end{aligned}
The survival function falls from a left limit 9/169/16 to 0 at the cap. Its value at that one integration endpoint does not change either integral. No extra atom term is needed in this method: the full-cap outcomes contribute to P(W>t)P(W>t) at every threshold below the cap.

The two full-cap and no-meeting events differ only by {D=1/4}\{D=1/4\}, a null event here. That explains their equal probabilities without asserting that meeting at exactly the cap is impossible as an outcome.
For another cap aa, the same procedure uses the event {min⁡(D,a)≤w}\{\min(D,a)\le w\}, splits the law into the continuous component below aa and its mass at aa, and computes moments from the complete law. The accompanying sliders keep the independent uniform arrival measure fixed while changing this policy. Similar calculations describe capped losses or a sensor reading limited by a display ceiling. Capping keeps the affected outcomes and records the limit; it is different from discarding observations above a threshold.


A.13. Independent exercises
A1. A 30-minute allowance. Define W=min⁡(D,1/2)W=\min(D,1/2). Construct its CDF, specify its continuous component and point mass, and calculate its mean. State the units of your answer.
A2. A general allowance. For 0<a<10<a<1, define Wa=min⁡(D,a)W_a=\min(D,a). Derive the mass at aa, the first and second moments, and the variance as functions of aa. Check their limits as a↓0a\downarrow0 and a↑1a\uparrow1.
A3. Uncapped versus capped. Calculate the mean and variance of the gap DD, and compare them with those of W=min⁡(D,1/4)W=\min(D,1/4). Use the transformations to explain the changes; keep hours and minutes consistent.
A4. Conditional waiting. Given that the friends meet, calculate E[W∣D≤1/4]E[W\mid D\le1/4]. Identify the conditioning probability, normalize the restricted law, and explain why the result differs from the unconditional mean.
A5. Simulation. Generate 10,000 independent pairs (TA,i,TB,i)(T_{A,i},T_{B,i}) with independent uniform coordinates. Record Di=|TA,i−TB,i|D_i=|T_{A,i}-T_{B,i}| and Wi=min⁡(Di,1/4)W_i=\min(D_i,1/4). Estimate the meeting probability, the full-cap frequency, the mean wait and its variance. State your seed and whether the variance calculation uses denominator nn or n−1n-1. Compare with the analytic results and explain why finite-sample estimates need not agree exactly. When plotting, show the atom separately instead of interpreting a histogram spike as an ordinary PDF height.
For the general theory behind the moment calculations, see 01.5: expectation and variance. For inverse images, Jacobians and mixed transformed laws, see 01.6: transformations. The distribution-theory supplement derives the uncapped gap density for both arrival models.

title: 01.5 · Expectation, mean and variance
text:
Questions and objectives
Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu
Previous: meeting problem · Rigorous supplement · Next: transformations
A service team needs to budget reviewer time. A reliability engineer needs to distinguish consistent performance from occasional large deviations. An evaluation lead needs to combine results from task groups with different frequencies. A distribution answers probability questions; expectation summarizes specified numerical functions of that distribution.
We will define expectation for discrete and continuous variables, identify the mean and variance, calculate expectations of functions, and use covariance and conditional expectation. All datasets and application models are hypothetical. Worked examples include solutions; practice checks are for independent work.

text:
1. Begin with a weighted workload

Worked example: reviewer time per request
Select one request under a stipulated model. Let XX be the additional review time in minutes. The possible values and probabilities are:



xx (minutes)
0
2
5




pX(x)p_X(x)
0.5
0.3
0.2


xpX(x)x p_X(x)
0
0.6
1.0



For planning, weight each possible time by its probability:
0(0.5)+2(0.3)+5(0.2)=1.6 minutes per request.0(0.5)+2(0.3)+5(0.2)=1.6\text{ minutes per request}.
This is not a claim that any request takes 1.6 minutes. In this model no request does. It is a probability-weighted average. If 100 requests each have this marginal distribution, their expected total additional review time is 100(1.6)=160100(1.6)=160 minutes. Their realized total can differ, and independence has not yet been assumed.


Definition: expectation and mean
Let XX be a real random variable on (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P). Its expectation, also called its mean, is
μX=E[X]=∫ΩX(ω)dP(ω),\mu_X=E[X]=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,dP(\omega),
when E[|X|]<∞E[|X|]<\infty. For calculations using the induced distribution,
E[X]=∑xxpX(x)(discrete),E[X]=∫−∞∞xfX(x)dx(a density exists).E[X]=\sum_x x p_X(x)\quad\text{(discrete)},\qquad
E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x f_X(x)\,dx\quad\text{(a density exists)}.
The sum or integral must converge absolutely for a finite expectation. A nonnegative variable may have expectation +∞+\infty. For signed variables, cancellation of divergent positive and negative contributions does not define a mean. The supplement gives a boundary example.
The units of the mean are the units of XX. In the workload example, E[X]=1.6E[X]=1.6 minutes. The PMF supplies the weights; it is not an ordinary average of the distinct possible values, which would incorrectly give (0+2+5)/3(0+2+5)/3.
A sample mean X‾n=(X1+⋯+Xn)/n\bar X_n=(X_1+\cdots+X_n)/n is a statistic computed from observations; the model mean μX\mu_X is a property of a probability law. For independent, identically distributed observations with finite absolute mean, the law of large numbers gives a long-run interpretation. A small sample need not have an average near μX\mu_X; convergence is developed in Module 02.
Practice check E1. A hypothetical invoice correction cost is 0, 100 or 400 rupees with probabilities 0.7,0.2,0.10.7,0.2,0.1. Calculate its mean and explain why averaging the three cost values without weights answers a different question.

2. Continuous expectation

Worked example: the gap between the friends’ arrivals
In the independent uniform-arrival model from 01.4, the gap D=|TA−TB|D=|T_A-T_B| has density fD(d)=2(1−d)f_D(d)=2(1-d) for 0<d<10<d<1, zero elsewhere. What is the mean gap?
E[D]=∫01d2(1−d)dd=2∫01(d−d2)dd=2[d22−d33]01=13 hour=20 minutes.\begin{aligned}
E[D]&=\int_0^1 d\,2(1-d)\,dd
=2\int_0^1(d-d^2)\,dd\\
&=2\left[\frac{d^2}{2}-\frac{d^3}{3}\right]_0^1
=\frac13\text{ hour}=20\text{ minutes}.
\end{aligned}
The integrand is value times density. Density alone integrates to probability; multiplying by the value before integrating gives its probability-weighted mean. This is the mean arrival gap, not the first friend’s actual waiting time, which is capped at 15 minutes by the policy.


Worked example: actual waiting time
The fully worked meeting-problem appendix derives the complete CDF, its jump, and both moments step by step.
Let W=min⁡(D,1/4)W=\min(D,1/4) be the time the first arrival spends waiting. If the gap is below 1/41/4, the wait equals the gap; otherwise it is 1/41/4 even though the friends fail to meet. Then
E[W]=∫01/4d2(1−d)dd+14∫1/412(1−d)dd=596+14916=37192 hour=11.5625 minutes.\begin{aligned}
E[W]
&=\int_0^{1/4}d\,2(1-d)\,dd
+\frac14\int_{1/4}^1 2(1-d)\,dd\\
&=\frac5{96}+\frac14\frac9{16}
=\frac{37}{192}\text{ hour}
=11.5625\text{ minutes}.
\end{aligned}
This calculation motivates the expectation-of-a-function rule (often called LOTUS). For an integrable measurable g(X)g(X),
E[g(X)]=∑xg(x)pX(x)quadorE[g(X)]=∫g(x)fX(x)dx.E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x)quad\text{or}\quad
E[g(X)]=\int g(x)f_X(x)\,dx.
We do not need to derive the distribution of g(X)g(X) first. In fact WW has a point mass at 1/41/4, so treating it as having only a smooth PDF would miss part of its law.
For a pair with a joint density, the corresponding formula is
E[g(X,Y)]=∬g(x,y)fX,Y(x,y)dxdy,E[g(X,Y)]=\iint g(x,y)f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy,
provided the same integral with |g||g| is finite. Replace the double integral by a double sum for a joint PMF.

3. Variance: distinguish means from variability

Same mean, different performance
Suppose system A always takes two seconds, while system B takes one or three seconds with equal probability. Both means are two seconds. Their mean signed deviations are zero, so signed deviations cannot measure spread. Squaring the deviations gives 0 for A and 1 square second for B.
For a variable with finite second moment, the variance and standard deviation are
Var⁡(X)=E[(X−μX)2],SD⁡(X)=Var⁡(X).\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu_X)^2],\qquad
\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
Variance is nonnegative and has squared units; standard deviation has the original units. Expanding the square gives the computational identity
Var⁡(X)=E[X2]−(E[X])2.\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2.
The mean is the first raw moment; E[X2]E[X^2] is the second raw moment; variance is the second moment about the mean. A zero variance means X=μXX=\mu_X with probability 1.


Worked example: reviewer-time variance
For the initial PMF,
E[X2]=02(0.5)+22(0.3)+52(0.2)=6.2.E[X^2]=0^2(0.5)+2^2(0.3)+5^2(0.2)=6.2.
Therefore
Var⁡(X)=6.2−1.62=3.64 minutes2,SD⁡(X)=3.64≈1.908 minutes.\operatorname{Var}(X)=6.2-1.6^2=3.64\text{ minutes}^2,
\qquad\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{3.64}\approx1.908\text{ minutes}.
Check directly:
0.5(0−1.6)2+0.3(2−1.6)2+0.2(5−1.6)2=1.28+0.048+2.312=3.64.0.5(0-1.6)^2+0.3(2-1.6)^2+0.2(5-1.6)^2
=1.28+0.048+2.312=3.64.
Variance summarizes spread about the mean. It does not by itself specify a tail probability or guarantee a service deadline.


Worked example: continuous gap variance
For the arrival gap,
E[D2]=2∫01(d2−d3)dd=2(13−14)=16.E[D^2]=2\int_0^1(d^2-d^3)\,dd
=2\left(\frac13-\frac14\right)=\frac16.
Thus
Var⁡(D)=16−19=118 hour2.\operatorname{Var}(D)=\frac16-\frac19=\frac1{18}\text{ hour}^2.
If Dm=60DD_m=60D is the gap in minutes, its mean is 20 minutes and its variance is 602/18=20060^2/18=200 minutes squared. Its standard deviation is 200≈14.142\sqrt{200}\approx14.142 minutes.
Practice check E2. Let UU have density 1/41/4 on [0,4][0,4] seconds. Calculate E[U]E[U], E[U2]E[U^2], its variance and standard deviation. State the units at each step.
Stopping point. Students should be able to calculate and distinguish E[X2]E[X^2] and (E[X])2(E[X])^2 before proceeding.

4. Linear combinations and covariance

Convert a workload into a cost
If a processing charge is C=10+3XC=10+3X rupees, with XX measured in minutes, then the initial workload model gives
E[C]=10+3(1.6)=14.8 rupees,Var⁡(C)=32(3.64)=32.76 rupees2.E[C]=10+3(1.6)=14.8\text{ rupees},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(C)=3^2(3.64)=32.76\text{ rupees}^2.
In general, for integrable variables,
E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c.E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c.
Linearity needs no independence. For finite second moments, Var⁡(aX+b)=a2Var⁡(X)\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X). Adding a fixed amount shifts the mean but does not change spread.


Why two duration variances may not add
In the triangular support-ticket model, fX,Y(x,y)=1/2f_{X,Y}(x,y)=1/2 on 0<y<x<20<y<x<2. The marginals are fX(x)=x/2f_X(x)=x/2 and fY(y)=(2−y)/2f_Y(y)=(2-y)/2 on (0,2)(0,2). Direct integration gives
E[X]=∫02x22dx=43,E[Y]=∫02y(2−y)2dy=23,E[X]=\int_0^2\frac{x^2}{2}\,dx=\frac43,\quad
E[Y]=\int_0^2\frac{y(2-y)}2\,dy=\frac23,
E[X2]=2,E[Y2]=23,E[X^2]=2,\qquad E[Y^2]=\frac23,
and hence both variances are 2/92/9. For the total duration, we also need
E[XY]=∫02∫0xxy2dydx=∫02x34dx=1.E[XY]=\int_0^2\int_0^x\frac{xy}{2}\,dy\,dx
=\int_0^2\frac{x^3}{4}\,dx=1.
The covariance is
Cov⁡(X,Y)=E[(X−E[X])(Y−E[Y])]=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y].\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])]=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y].
Here it is 1−(4/3)(2/3)=1/91-(4/3)(2/3)=1/9 hours squared. Expanding a squared sum gives
Var⁡(aX+bY)=a2Var⁡(X)+b2Var⁡(Y)+2abCov⁡(X,Y).\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).
For T=X+YT=X+Y, E[T]=2E[T]=2 hours and
Var⁡(T)=29+29+219=23 hours2.\operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac29+\frac29+2\frac19=\frac23\text{ hours}^2.
Omitting covariance would give 4/94/9, an incorrect result for this model. When both variances are positive, correlation is
ρX,Y=Cov⁡(X,Y)SD⁡(X)SD⁡(Y);\rho_{X,Y}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{SD}(X)\operatorname{SD}(Y)};
here it is 1/21/2. Correlation is dimensionless and lies in [−1,1][-1,1]. Independence implies zero covariance when second moments exist; the converse generally fails.


Worked distinction: uncorrelated does not mean independent
Let UU be uniform on [−1,1][-1,1] and V=U2V=U^2. Symmetry gives E[U]=E[U3]=0E[U]=E[U^3]=0, so Cov⁡(U,V)=0\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)=0. Yet VV is determined by UU. More explicitly, the events |U|≤1/2|U|\le1/2 and V≤1/4V\le1/4 are identical, each with probability 1/21/2; their intersection has probability 1/21/2, not 1/41/4.
Practice check E3. A daily total is the sum of 20 independent request costs, each with mean 14.8 and variance 32.76. Find the mean and variance of the total. Which calculation remains valid if independence is removed but each marginal distribution is retained?

title: 01.5 · Expectation, mean and variance
section: 5. Conditional means and changing task populations
text:
5. Conditional means and changing task populations

Worked example: two task groups
Let GG denote the type of a randomly selected task. Stipulate P(G=routine)=0.75P(G=\mathrm{routine})=0.75 and P(G=complex)=0.25P(G=\mathrm{complex})=0.25. The review-time means within these groups are 2 and 6 minutes; their variances are 1 and 4 minutes squared.
Weight the group means by group probabilities:
E[X]=0.75(2)+0.25(6)=3 minutes.E[X]=0.75(2)+0.25(6)=3\text{ minutes}.
A conditional mean is the expectation under a conditional distribution:
m(g)=E[X∣G=g]=∑xxpX∣G(x∣g)m(g)=E[X\mid G=g]=\sum_x x p_{X\mid G}(x\mid g)
or its density integral, where defined. The random variable m(G)=E[X∣G]m(G)=E[X\mid G] assigns each outcome its group’s mean. The law of total expectation is
E[X]=E[E[X∣G]].E[X]=E[E[X\mid G]].
For finite second moments, the law of total variance is
Var⁡(X)=E[Var⁡(X∣G)]+Var⁡(E[X∣G]).\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid G)]+\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid G]).
Here the within-group term is 0.75(1)+0.25(4)=1.750.75(1)+0.25(4)=1.75. The between-group term is
0.75(2−3)2+0.25(6−3)2=0.75+2.25=3.0.75(2-3)^2+0.25(6-3)^2=0.75+2.25=3.
The total variance is 4.754.75 minutes squared. Averaging the conditional variances alone would miss variability due to the different group means. A change in task proportions can change the overall mean and variance even when each group’s performance is unchanged.


Continuous conditioning in the support-ticket triangle
The conditional density of YY given X=xX=x is 1/x1/x on (0,x)(0,x), for 0<x<20<x<2. Consequently,
E[Y∣X=x]=∫0xy1xdy=x2.E[Y\mid X=x]=\int_0^x y\frac1x\,dy=\frac x2.
Using the marginal of XX,
E[E[Y∣X]]=∫02x2x2dx=23,E[E[Y\mid X]]=\int_0^2\frac x2\frac x2\,dx=\frac23,
which agrees with the direct calculation of E[Y]E[Y]. This is conditioning through a density version, not division by P(X=x)=0P(X=x)=0.
Practice check E4. Change the routine-task probability to 1/21/2, retaining the two group means and variances. Find the new overall mean and variance.

text:
6. Expectations of indicators and generating functions
A review passes with stipulated probability pp. Let I=1I=1 for a pass and 0 otherwise. Then
E[I]=0(1−p)+1p=p,Var⁡(I)=p−p2=p(1−p).E[I]=0(1-p)+1p=p,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(I)=p-p^2=p(1-p).
This gives the general identity E[𝟏A]=P(A)E[\mathbf1_A]=P(A). A sum of indicators counts occurrences, so its expected count is the sum of the occurrence probabilities, even when the indicators are dependent.
For a nonnegative integer-valued count NN, the probability generating function is GN(s)=E[sN]=∑n≥0pN(n)snG_N(s)=E[s^N]=\sum_{n\ge0}p_N(n)s^n for 0≤s≤10\le s\le1. For the reviewer-count PMF P(N=0,1,2)=(0.5,0.3,0.2)P(N=0,1,2)=(0.5,0.3,0.2),
GN(s)=0.5+0.3s+0.2s2,GN′(1)=0.7=E[N].G_N(s)=0.5+0.3s+0.2s^2,\qquad G_N'(1)=0.7=E[N].
Also GN″(1)=0.4=E[N(N−1)]G_N''(1)=0.4=E[N(N-1)], so Var⁡(N)=0.4+0.7−0.72=0.61\operatorname{Var}(N)=0.4+0.7-0.7^2=0.61. For infinite supports, derivatives at 1 are understood as left limits with the relevant finite-moment assumptions. The supplement also defines the moment generating function; it need not exist near zero for every law.
Practice check E5. For a Bernoulli indicator with success probability 0.80.8, write its PGF and use it to calculate the mean and variance.

Questions and objectives
Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu
Previous: expectation · Rigorous supplement · Next: multivariate normal
A service manager records two phase durations but needs the distribution of their sum. An engineer records a signed error but reports its square. In the friends’ meeting problem, the decision depends on the absolute gap rather than the two separate arrival times.
In each case, the experiment and its probability measure remain fixed while a new function records a different value. We will derive transformed laws by constructing inverse-image events and integrating, by constructing a joint density with an auxiliary variable, and by applying Jacobians. All application models are stipulated for teaching.

title: 01.6 · Transformations of random variables
section: 1. Start from the event: the CDF method
text:
1. Start from the event: the CDF method

Worked example: square a signed measurement error
Let XX be a hypothetical sensor error, uniform on [−2,2][-2,2] in a specified measurement unit. The reporting system uses squared error Y=X2Y=X^2. What is P(Y≤1)P(Y\le1)?
The condition X2≤1X^2\le1 selects −1≤X≤1-1\le X\le1, an interval of length 2 within an interval of length 4. Thus P(Y≤1)=1/2P(Y\le1)=1/2. For a general threshold 0≤y≤40\le y\le4,
{Y≤y}={−y≤X≤y},FY(y)=∫−yy14dx=y2.\{Y\le y\}=\{-\sqrt y\le X\le\sqrt y\},\qquad
F_Y(y)=\int_{-\sqrt y}^{\sqrt y}\frac14\,dx=\frac{\sqrt y}{2}.
Including thresholds outside the range,
FY(y)={0,y<0,y/2,0≤y≤4,1,y>4.F_Y(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y<0,\\\sqrt y/2,&0\le y\le4,\\1,&y>4.\end{cases}
Differentiation gives
fY(y)=14y,0<y<4,f_Y(y)=\frac1{4\sqrt y},\qquad0<y<4,
and zero elsewhere. The density is unbounded near zero but integrable: ∫04(4y)−1dy=1\int_0^4(4\sqrt y)^{-1}dy=1. There is no atom at zero since P(X=0)=0P(X=0)=0.


General construction
For measurable gg, define Y=g(X)Y=g(X). Its induced law is
PY(B)=P(g(X)∈B),FY(y)=P(g(X)≤y).P_Y(B)=P(g(X)\in B),\qquad F_Y(y)=P(g(X)\le y).
If XX has a density,
FY(y)=∫{x:g(x)≤y}fX(x)dx.F_Y(y)=\int_{\{x:g(x)\le y\}}f_X(x)\,dx.
For Z=g(X,Y)Z=g(X,Y) and an available joint density,
FZ(z)=∬{(x,y):g(x,y)≤z}fX,Y(x,y)dxdy.F_Z(z)=\iint_{\{(x,y):g(x,y)\le z\}}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
First identify the transformed range, then the inverse-image region and its bounds, then integrate. Differentiate the CDF where appropriate only after checking whether the transformed law has atoms. A smooth PDF is not guaranteed merely because the original variable has one.
Practice check T1. For the same XX, find the CDF and PDF of |X||X|. Include the thresholds outside its range and verify normalization.

title: 01.6 · Transformations of random variables
text:
2. A one-dimensional Jacobian

Worked example: convert and shift a duration
Let XX be uniform on [0,2][0,2] hours and Y=10+60XY=10+60X minutes. Then 10<Y<13010<Y<130 and x=(y−10)/60x=(y-10)/60. Since a one-minute interval of YY corresponds to 1/601/60 hour of XX,
fY(y)=fX(y−1060)|dxdy|=12160=1120.f_Y(y)=f_X\left(\frac{y-10}{60}\right)\left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right|
=\frac12\frac1{60}=\frac1{120}.
It integrates to 1 over an interval of length 120. Changing the numerical scale changes density height, preserving probabilities.
If gg is a differentiable, strictly monotone map with a differentiable inverse hh and nonzero derivative on the relevant support interior, the change-of-variable formula is
fY(y)=fX(h(y))|h′(y)|,f_Y(y)=f_X(h(y))\,|h'(y)|,
on the transformed support and zero elsewhere. The multiplier is the absolute derivative of the inverse transformation. Endpoint exceptions of probability zero can be treated separately.
For a transformation with finitely many smooth inverse branches, add their contributions:
fY(y)=∑x:g(x)=yfX(x)|g′(x)|,f_Y(y)=\sum_{x:g(x)=y}\frac{f_X(x)}{|g'(x)|},
at regular values with nonzero derivatives. For Y=X2Y=X^2 and 0<y<40<y<4, there are two roots ±y\pm\sqrt y:
fY(y)=1/42y+1/42y=14y.f_Y(y)=\frac{1/4}{2\sqrt y}+\frac{1/4}{2\sqrt y}=\frac1{4\sqrt y}.
Using only the positive root would lose half the probability. At the critical value zero, use the CDF to check for an atom rather than substituting into the branch formula.

section: 4. Construct a joint density, then marginalize
text:
4. Construct a joint density, then marginalize

Rework the sum using an auxiliary variable
A map from two values to their sum loses information. To use a square Jacobian matrix, retain an auxiliary variable: set
S=X+Y,V=X.S=X+Y,\qquad V=X.
The inverse is x=vx=v, y=s−vy=s-v. Its Jacobian matrix and absolute determinant are
∂(x,y)∂(s,v)=(011−1),|det⁡|=1.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,v)}=
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad |\det|=1.
The original inequalities 0<x<10<x<1, 0<y<10<y<1 become
0<v<1,0<s−v<1⇔max⁡(0,s−1)<v<min⁡(1,s).0<v<1,\quad0<s-v<1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \max(0,s-1)<v<\min(1,s).
Thus fS,V(s,v)=1f_{S,V}(s,v)=1 on that region and zero elsewhere. Integrate out vv:
fS(s)=∫max⁡(0,s−1)min⁡(1,s)1dv,f_S(s)=\int_{\max(0,s-1)}^{\min(1,s)}1\,dv,
when the upper bound exceeds the lower. The width is ss for 0<s<10<s<1 and 2−s2-s for 1<s<21<s<2, reproducing the CDF result.
For a general joint density, the same construction gives
fX+Y(s)=∫−∞∞fX,Y(v,s−v)dv.f_{X+Y}(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(v,s-v)\,dv.
Under independence, this becomes the convolution formula
fX+Y(s)=∫−∞∞fX(v)fY(s−v)dv.f_{X+Y}(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_X(v)f_Y(s-v)\,dv.
Dependence does not prevent the first formula; it prevents replacing the joint density by the product without justification.


Formal two-dimensional change of variables
Suppose (X,Y)(X,Y) has a joint density and the transformation (U,V)=g(X,Y)(U,V)=g(X,Y) is a one-to-one continuously differentiable map between open support regions, with continuously differentiable inverse (x,y)=h(u,v)(x,y)=h(u,v) and nonzero Jacobian determinant. Then
fU,V(u,v)=fX,Y(h(u,v))|det∂(x,y)∂(u,v)|.f_{U,V}(u,v)=f_{X,Y}(h(u,v))
\left|\det\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|.
A small region in the new coordinates corresponds to an old-coordinate area multiplied by the inverse determinant. Probability is preserved, so density acquires that factor. State the transformed support as part of the result. Null boundaries can be omitted; branch maps require adding branch contributions. A dimension-reducing map such as (x,y)↦x+y(x,y)\mapsto x+y has no square determinant by itself.
Practice check T2. For independent U(0,1)U(0,1) inputs, use R=X−YR=X-Y, V=YV=Y to obtain a joint density and then the density of RR. Show the support inequalities explicitly.
