5. A nonconstant Jacobian: total duration and its share

Worked example: time spent in the first of two phases
Let X,YX,Y be independent with density e−xe^{-x} on x>0x>0, zero otherwise, using a time unit in which the rate is 1. This exponential model is a stipulation. Define
S=X+Y,R=XX+Y.S=X+Y,\qquad R=\frac{X}{X+Y}.
The total is positive and the fraction lies between 0 and 1. The inverse map is x=rsx=rs, y=(1−r)sy=(1-r)s. Compute rather than guess the determinant:
∂(x,y)∂(s,r)=(rs1−r−s),det⁡=−rs−s(1−r)=−s.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,r)}=
\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\1-r&-s\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det=-rs-s(1-r)=-s.
Thus
fS,R(s,r)=e−rse−(1−r)ss=se−s,s>0,0<r<1.f_{S,R}(s,r)=e^{-rs}e^{-(1-r)s}s=se^{-s},\quad s>0,\ 0<r<1.
Marginalization gives
fS(s)=∫01se−sdr=se−s,fR(r)=∫0∞se−sds=1.f_S(s)=\int_0^1se^{-s}\,dr=se^{-s},\qquad
f_R(r)=\int_0^\infty se^{-s}\,ds=1.
Integration by parts yields ∫0∞se−sds=1\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1. The joint density factors into its marginals on the product support, so the total and share are independent in this particular model. This conclusion depends on the stipulated equal-rate exponential inputs; it does not follow from the definitions of total and share alone.
For example,
P(S≤2,R≤1/4)=∫02∫01/4se−sdrds=14[1−3e−2].P(S\le2,R\le1/4)=\int_0^2\int_0^{1/4}se^{-s}\,dr\,ds
=\frac14[1-3e^{-2}].

6. Return to the meeting-time gap
For independent uniform arrivals TA,TBT_A,T_B in [0,1][0,1], take the signed difference Z=TB−TAZ=T_B-T_A and retain V=TAV=T_A. Then tA=vt_A=v, tB=v+zt_B=v+z and the inverse determinant has absolute value 1. The joint support is
max⁡(0,−z)<v<min⁡(1,1−z).\max(0,-z)<v<\min(1,1-z).
Integrating its width gives fZ(z)=1−|z|f_Z(z)=1-|z| for −1<z<1-1<z<1. The absolute gap D=|Z|D=|Z| has two preimages for d>0d>0, so
fD(d)=fZ(d)+fZ(−d)=2(1−d),0<d<1.f_D(d)=f_Z(d)+f_Z(-d)=2(1-d),\quad0<d<1.
This agrees with the band-area CDF route in 01.4. Both routes construct the same induced law under the same original measure.

7. Generate variables by transforming simple ones

Worked example: generate a nonuniform arrival time
Let U∼U(0,1)U\sim U(0,1) and define T=1−1−UT=1-\sqrt{1-U}. For 0≤t≤10\le t\le1,
P(T≤t)=P(1−1−U≤t)=P(U≤1−(1−t)2)=2t−t2.\begin{aligned}
P(T\le t)&=P(1-\sqrt{1-U}\le t)\\
&=P(U\le1-(1-t)^2)=2t-t^2.
\end{aligned}
Differentiation gives fT(t)=2(1−t)f_T(t)=2(1-t), the early-arrival model. Two independent uniform inputs transformed separately produce independent arrivals with these marginals.
More generally, for a CDF FF define its generalized inverse F−1(u)=inf⁡{x:F(x)≥u}F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\} for 0<u<10<u<1. Then F−1(U)F^{-1}(U) has CDF FF. The generalized inverse also handles discrete laws: if P(N=0,1,2)=(0.5,0.3,0.2)P(N=0,1,2)=(0.5,0.3,0.2), assign 0 for U<0.5U<0.5, 1 for 0.5≤U<0.80.5\le U<0.8, and 2 otherwise.
Generating both variables from the same uniform input can create dependence even when both marginals are correct. The multivariate-normal construction in 01.7 will deliberately combine independent inputs to obtain a chosen covariance.

Return to DD and define the capped wait W=min⁡(D,1/4)W=\min(D,1/4). For 0≤w<1/40\le w<1/4, FW(w)=2w−w2F_W(w)=2w-w^2. At and above 1/41/4, FW(w)=1F_W(w)=1. The CDF jumps by
1−FW((1/4)−)=1−716=916.1-F_W((1/4)^-)=1-\frac7{16}=\frac9{16}.
Thus WW has a continuous component on (0,1/4)(0,1/4) and a point mass 9/169/16 at 1/41/4. Differentiating away from the jump cannot recover that atom. This is why the CDF and inverse-image construction is the general starting point.

title: 01.7 · The multivariate normal distribution
text:
Questions and objectives
Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu
Previous: transformations · Rigorous supplement · Module overview
Two sensors measure deviations from their calibration targets. Each deviation can be positive or negative. If they share an environmental disturbance, large values may occur together. Knowing each marginal distribution does not determine the probability of simultaneous deviations or the distribution of one sensor after observing the other.
We will construct a multivariate normal vector, define its density and covariance matrix, derive its two-dimensional form, and use its marginals, conditional laws and linear transformations. We will interpret density contours and generate correlated observations. All sensor and financial models below are hypothetical; a normal law is an assumption to examine, not a conclusion from a mean and covariance alone.

7  01.7 · The multivariate normal distribution

title: 01.7 · The multivariate normal distribution
text:
1. Build two related measurements

A numerical model before the general definition
Let Z1,Z2Z_1,Z_2 be independent standard normal variables, each with density
ϕ(z)=12πe−z2/2,z∈ℝ.\phi(z)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2},\qquad z\in\mathbb R.
This is the one-dimensional normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1. In general, N(μ,σ2)N(\mu,\sigma^2) has mean μ\mu, variance σ2>0\sigma^2>0, and density ϕ((x−μ)/σ)/σ\phi((x-\mu)/\sigma)/\sigma.
Define two sensor errors in a common measurement unit:
X1=Z1,X2=Z1+3Z2.X_1=Z_1,\qquad X_2=Z_1+\sqrt3 Z_2.
Linearity of expectation gives both means zero. Independence gives
Var⁡(X1)=1,Var⁡(X2)=1+3=4,\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=1,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_2)=1+3=4,
Cov⁡(X1,X2)=E[Z1(Z1+3Z2)]=1.\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=E[Z_1(Z_1+\sqrt3Z_2)]=1.
Their correlation is 1/(1⋅2)=1/21/(1\cdot2)=1/2. The term Z1Z_1 shared by the two formulas creates covariance. If we know X1=1X_1=1, the natural conditional model is X2=1+3Z2X_2=1+\sqrt3 Z_2, giving conditional mean 1 and variance 3. We will justify this using the joint density later in the lecture.


Mean vector and covariance matrix
For a column vector 𝑿=(X1,…,Xp)T\mathbf X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)^T with finite second moments, define
𝝁=E[𝑿],Σ=E[(𝑿−𝝁)(𝑿−𝝁)T].\boldsymbol\mu=E[\mathbf X],\qquad
\Sigma=E[(\mathbf X-\boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf X-\boldsymbol\mu)^T].
The diagonal entries are variances; entry (i,j)(i,j) is Cov⁡(Xi,Xj)\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j). In the sensor model,
𝝁=(00),Σ=(1114).\boldsymbol\mu=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}.
Every covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite: for any vector aa, aTΣa=Var⁡(aT𝑿)≥0a^T\Sigma a=\operatorname{Var}(a^T\mathbf X)\ge0. Positive definite means this is strictly positive for every nonzero aa; it excludes a linear combination with zero variance.

title: 01.7 · The multivariate normal distribution
text:
2. Definition and density
A vector is multivariate normal, or jointly Gaussian, if every linear combination aT𝑿a^T\mathbf X is a univariate normal variable, allowing a constant as a degenerate normal. Equivalently, it can be represented as
𝑿=𝝁+A𝒁,\mathbf X=\boldsymbol\mu+A\mathbf Z,
where 𝒁\mathbf Z has independent standard normal components. Its covariance is AATAA^T. We write 𝑿∼Np(𝝁,Σ)\mathbf X\sim N_p(\boldsymbol\mu,\Sigma).
For a positive definite p×pp\times p covariance matrix, the joint density is
f𝑿(𝒙)=1(2π)p/2|Σ|1/2exp⁡[−12(𝒙−𝝁)TΣ−1(𝒙−𝝁)],𝒙∈ℝp.f_{\mathbf X}(\mathbf x)=
\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}}
\exp\left[-\frac12(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)\right],
\qquad\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^p.
Here |Σ||\Sigma| denotes the determinant. A canonical probability model is (ℝp,ℬ(ℝp),P)(\mathbb R^p,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^p),P) with P(B)=∫Bf𝑿(𝒙)d𝒙P(B)=\int_B f_{\mathbf X}(\mathbf x)d\mathbf x and coordinate random variables. The density is nonnegative and integrates to 1. It is not the probability of a point, which is zero.
To see where the formula comes from, choose an invertible LL with LLT=ΣLL^T=\Sigma, and transform independent standard normals by 𝒙=𝝁+L𝒛\mathbf x=\boldsymbol\mu+L\mathbf z. The inverse Jacobian factor is 1/|det⁡L|=1/|Σ|1/|\det L|=1/\sqrt{|\Sigma|}, and 𝒛T𝒛=(𝒙−𝝁)TΣ−1(𝒙−𝝁)\mathbf z^T\mathbf z=(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu). This applies the previous lecture’s change-of-variables rule. The supplement supplies the full normalization argument.

Worked example: evaluate and interpret a density
For the sensor covariance,
|Σ|=4−1=3,Σ−1=13(4−1−11).|\Sigma|=4-1=3,\qquad
\Sigma^{-1}=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
At 𝒙=(1,2)T\mathbf x=(1,2)^T, the quadratic form is
q=13(4(1)2−2(1)(2)+(2)2)=43.q=\frac13(4(1)^2-2(1)(2)+(2)^2)=\frac43.
Therefore
f(1,2)=12π3e−2/3≈0.04718.f(1,2)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt3}e^{-2/3}\approx0.04718.
This is a density in inverse squared measurement units. A small rectangle centered there with widths h1,h2h_1,h_2 has probability approximately f(1,2)h1h2f(1,2)h_1h_2 when the density varies little over it. The exact probability is its double integral, not 0.047180.04718.
Practice check N1. For the same model, evaluate the quadratic form and density at (1,−2)T(1,-2)^T. Explain the comparison with (1,2)T(1,2)^T using the sign of the covariance.

3. The two-dimensional formula and its geometry
Write
Σ=(σ12ρσ1σ2ρσ1σ2σ22),σ1,σ2>0,|ρ|<1.\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1^2&\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\\
\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2&\sigma_2^2
\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_1,\sigma_2>0,\quad |\rho|<1.
Its determinant is σ12σ22(1−ρ2)>0\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2(1-\rho^2)>0. Put zi=(xi−μi)/σiz_i=(x_i-\mu_i)/\sigma_i. The density becomes
f(x1,x2)=12πσ1σ21−ρ2exp⁡[−z12−2ρz1z2+z222(1−ρ2)].f(x_1,x_2)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_1\sigma_2\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}
\exp\left[-\frac{z_1^2-2\rho z_1z_2+z_2^2}{2(1-\rho^2)}\right].
At fixed density, the quadratic form q=(𝒙−𝝁)TΣ−1(𝒙−𝝁)q=(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu) is constant. If Σ=QΛQT\Sigma=Q\Lambda Q^T with orthonormal eigenvectors and positive eigenvalues λi\lambda_i, coordinates 𝒖=QT(𝒙−𝝁)\mathbf u=Q^T(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu) give
q=u12λ1+u22λ2.q=\frac{u_1^2}{\lambda_1}+\frac{u_2^2}{\lambda_2}.
Contours are ellipses centered at the mean, with principal directions given by the eigenvectors and semiaxis lengths cλi\sqrt{c\lambda_i} at q=cq=c. Positive correlation tilts contours toward pairs with matching signs of standardized deviations; negative correlation favors opposite signs. Marginal standard deviations and principal-axis standard deviations are generally different quantities.



Equal marginal variances with different correlations. Each outlined region contains 95% of the stipulated Gaussian probability.


Open the bivariate-normal density and conditioning explorer. Change correlation, means and scales. Compare the density heatmap and its contour with the marginal and conditional curves. The density color scale is displayed; use the numerical values when comparing models.

A contour is not itself a probability
For this bivariate normal law,
P(q≤c)=1−e−c/2,c≥0.P(q\le c)=1-e^{-c/2},\qquad c\ge0.
Thus the ellipse q≤1q\le1 contains about 39.35%39.35\%, not 68%68\%, of the probability. A 95% probability ellipse uses c=−2log⁡(0.05)≈5.991c=-2\log(0.05)\approx5.991. It describes the distribution of observations under known parameters; it is not automatically a confidence region for an estimated mean. The contour line itself has probability zero. The supplement derives the interior probability by polar integration.

4. Marginal and conditional normal laws

Marginals retain coordinates
Ignoring the second sensor in the construction gives X1=Z1∼N(0,1)X_1=Z_1\sim N(0,1). Ignoring the first gives X2=Z1+3Z2∼N(0,4)X_2=Z_1+\sqrt3Z_2\sim N(0,4). This illustrates the general property: every subvector of a jointly normal vector is normal, with the corresponding subvector of means and covariance submatrix.
The statement that X2X_2 is normal follows from joint normality of the independent normal inputs and the linear-combination property. Having normally shaped marginal distributions alone would not justify the full joint model.


Condition on one observed sensor
Complete the square in the bivariate exponent:
z12−2ρz1z2+z221−ρ2=z12+(z2−ρz1)21−ρ2.\frac{z_1^2-2\rho z_1z_2+z_2^2}{1-\rho^2}
=z_1^2+\frac{(z_2-\rho z_1)^2}{1-\rho^2}.
The joint density factors into the marginal density of X1X_1 and a normal density in X2X_2. Therefore a natural conditional version is
X2∣X1=x∼N(μ2+ρσ2σ1(x−μ1),σ22(1−ρ2)).X_2\mid X_1=x\sim N\left(
\mu_2+\rho\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}(x-\mu_1),\quad
\sigma_2^2(1-\rho^2)\right).
Conditioning shifts the mean linearly and reduces the variance unless ρ=0\rho=0. This is a density-based conditional law at a continuous value; it does not divide by the zero probability P(X1=x)P(X_1=x).
For the sensor model, μ1=μ2=0\mu_1=\mu_2=0, σ1=1\sigma_1=1, σ2=2\sigma_2=2, ρ=1/2\rho=1/2. At X1=1X_1=1,
E[X2∣X1=1]=1,Var⁡(X2∣X1=1)=4(1−1/4)=3.E[X_2\mid X_1=1]=1,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_2\mid X_1=1)=4(1-1/4)=3.
Let Φ(t)=∫−∞tϕ(z)dz\Phi(t)=\int_{-\infty}^t\phi(z)dz be the standard-normal CDF. A further probability calculation is
P(X2>2∣X1=1)=1−Φ(2−13)≈0.282,P(X_2>2\mid X_1=1)=1-\Phi\left(\frac{2-1}{\sqrt3}\right)\approx0.282,
whereas P(X2>2)=1−Φ(1)≈0.159P(X_2>2)=1-\Phi(1)\approx0.159. The conditioning information changes the question and the result; it does not establish a causal relation between sensors.
Practice check N2. In this sensor model, give the conditional mean and variance at X1=−1X_1=-1. Write P(X2>0∣X1=−1)P(X_2>0\mid X_1=-1) in terms of Φ\Phi.


Independence is a special normal-model property
For jointly normal scalar components, zero covariance is equivalent to independence. In the bivariate formula, ρ=0\rho=0 removes the cross term and makes the density the product of two marginal normal densities. The same principle applies to subvectors whose cross-covariance matrix is zero.
The qualification jointly normal matters. Let Z∼N(0,1)Z\sim N(0,1) and independently choose B=+1B=+1 or −1-1 with equal probabilities. Set X=ZX=Z, Y=BZY=BZ. Both marginals are standard normal and E[XY]=E[B]E[Z2]=0E[XY]=E[B]E[Z^2]=0. Yet |X|=|Y||X|=|Y| surely, so they are dependent. Also X+YX+Y has a point mass of 1/21/2 at zero and is not a nondegenerate normal variable. Thus the vector is not jointly normal.
Stopping point. Compare a marginal distribution, a conditional distribution, and the independence condition before applying matrix transformations.

5. Linear transformations, generation and whitening

Worked example: a weighted financial quantity
Suppose two modelled daily changes, in percentage points, are jointly normal with means 0.1 and 0.2, standard deviations 1 and 2, and correlation 1/21/2. Their covariance matrix is the sensor matrix. For R=0.6X1+0.4X2R=0.6X_1+0.4X_2,
E[R]=0.6(0.1)+0.4(0.2)=0.14,E[R]=0.6(0.1)+0.4(0.2)=0.14,
Var⁡(R)=0.62(1)+0.42(4)+2(0.6)(0.4)(1)=1.48.\operatorname{Var}(R)=0.6^2(1)+0.4^2(4)+2(0.6)(0.4)(1)=1.48.
Because this is a linear combination of jointly normal variables,
R∼N(0.14,1.48).R\sim N(0.14,1.48).
For example, P(R<0)=Φ(−0.14/1.48)≈0.454P(R<0)=\Phi(-0.14/\sqrt{1.48})\approx0.454. This is a calculation within an invented model, not a financial forecast. The mean and variance calculation is valid beyond normal distributions, but the conclusion that RR is normal needs the joint-normal assumption.
In general,
𝑿∼Np(𝝁,Σ)⇒A𝑿+b∼Nk(A𝝁+b,AΣAT).\mathbf X\sim N_p(\boldsymbol\mu,\Sigma)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A\mathbf X+b\sim N_k(A\boldsymbol\mu+b,A\Sigma A^T).
The new covariance may be singular, even if the original covariance is positive definite, when AA has deficient row rank.


Generate the desired covariance
For the two-dimensional parameterization, independent Z1,Z2∼N(0,1)Z_1,Z_2\sim N(0,1) give
X1=μ1+σ1Z1,X2=μ2+σ2(ρZ1+1−ρ2Z2).X_1=\mu_1+\sigma_1Z_1,\qquad
X_2=\mu_2+\sigma_2\left(\rho Z_1+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_2\right).
Then Cov⁡(X1,X2)=ρσ1σ2\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2, while the second variance is σ22[ρ2+(1−ρ2)]=σ22\sigma_2^2[\rho^2+(1-\rho^2)]=\sigma_2^2. This is the two-dimensional Cholesky construction 𝑿=𝝁+L𝒁\mathbf X=\boldsymbol\mu+L\mathbf Z.
Conversely, for invertible LL with LLT=ΣLL^T=\Sigma,
𝒁=L−1(𝑿−𝝁)∼Np(0,I).\mathbf Z=L^{-1}(\mathbf X-\boldsymbol\mu)\sim N_p(0,I).
This operation is called whitening. For the sensor example, Z1=X1Z_1=X_1 and Z2=(X2−X1)/3Z_2=(X_2-X_1)/\sqrt3. Dividing each original coordinate by its own standard deviation only standardizes the marginals; it leaves correlation 1/21/2 and does not whiten.
Open the generation and whitening demonstration. The same fixed simulated standard-normal pairs are transformed as correlation changes. Compare population covariance with the finite simulated sample covariance; they need not coincide exactly.
Practice check N3. For the sensor model, find the distribution of X2−X1X_2-X_1. Verify that its variance agrees with the construction in independent Z1,Z2Z_1,Z_2.

6. Boundary cases and what the model does not establish
At |ρ|=1|\rho|=1, |Σ|=0|\Sigma|=0 and the density formula involving Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} is unavailable. A Gaussian distribution can still exist: for example X2=2X1X_2=2X_1 with X1∼N(0,1)X_1\sim N(0,1) is concentrated on a line. It has no density with respect to two-dimensional area. The interactive density explorer restricts |ρ|<1|\rho|<1 so it always displays a genuine planar density.
A normal distribution has unbounded support. It can be a stipulated model for signed errors or changes, but using it for an inherently nonnegative duration requires considering the negative values it permits. Normal-looking marginals, an elliptical scatterplot, and a computed covariance do not by themselves prove joint normality. Distributional assumptions must be assessed using the context and data.

text:
1. Outcomes, events and mutual exclusivity
Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu
Module 01 · Fundamentals of Probability and Random Signal Theory
Supplement to 01.1 · Introduction to probability through problems
01.1 main materials
Supplementary materials
This supplement gives the formal definitions, parametrizations and derivations supporting the main lecture. Its details are intended for supplementary study alongside the corresponding lecture topics. For the chord calculations, RR is the fixed circle radius, TT the normalized midpoint distance, and LL the chord length, as in the Bertrand deck. The Billing indicator in the main notes remains XBX_B. All application records in this supplement are hypothetical teaching examples.
For the sigma-algebra discussion, follow the two-LED experiment, unit-interval model, generated sigma-algebras, and Vitali construction.
The main lecture motivates these constructions with questions about a hypothetical six-ticket routing audit, before introducing the triplet and axioms through finite calculations. The proofs below do not depend on that application; they state the general hypotheses needed for the results.
Reference: Krishna Jagannathan, Probability Foundations for Electrical Engineers, 9 July 2025, Chapters 1, 4 and 11, particularly Definitions 68–70 for measurable functions, random variables and their laws. The calculations of the sampling maps are written out below.
A sample space is required to satisfy two conditions. It must be exhaustive, so that at least one of its elements occurs in any realization of the experiment, and its elements must be mutually exclusive, so that at most one of them occurs. Together these state that exactly one ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega occurs each time the experiment is performed.
Distinct outcomes correspond to disjoint singleton subsets. When these singletons belong to the event collection, they are singleton events:
{ω1}∩{ω2}=⌀whenever ω1≠ω2.\{\omega_1\}\cap\{\omega_2\}=\varnothing\quad\text{whenever }\omega_1\ne\omega_2 .
For countable Ω\Omega the singletons therefore form a countable disjoint partition, Ω=⋃ω∈Ω{ω}\Omega=\bigcup_{\omega\in\Omega}\{\omega\} (a disjoint union).
Outcomes are mutually exclusive; events need not be. For a single roll of a die, Ω={1,2,3,4,5,6}\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}, and the outcomes 22 and 44 cannot both occur. The events
A={2,4,6}(even),B={4,5,6}(greater than 3)A=\{2,4,6\}\ \text{(even)},\qquad B=\{4,5,6\}\ \text{(greater than 3)}
can both occur, since A∩B={4,6}≠⌀A\cap B=\{4,6\}\ne\varnothing.

8  01.1 supplement · Sets, measurable maps and Bertrand's paradox

title: 01.1 supplement · Sets, measurable maps and Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Consequences for calculation
The two cases are handled by different rules, and the distinction above is what separates them.
Because singletons are disjoint, countable additivity applies directly to them, and for a countable event AA whose singletons are measurable
P(A)=∑ω∈AP({ω}).P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\}).
For two events no such rule is available, since additivity requires disjointness. The correction term is the shared part:
P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
Writing P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B) for the die events above would count the outcomes 44 and 66 twice.


Two errors that this distinction prevents
A list of events is not a sample space. For one roll of a die, the pair “even” and “greater than 3” is not a sample space: both can occur in a single roll, so the second condition fails. They are events in the finer space {1,…,6}\{1,\ldots,6\}.
A valid sample space need not have equally likely elements. For two independent fair tosses, the list “a head on the first toss”, “a tail then a head”, “two tails” is exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so it is a legitimate sample space. Its members carry probabilities 1/21/2, 1/41/4 and 1/41/4: they group the equally likely ordered outcomes as {HH,HT}\{HH,HT\}, {TH}\{TH\} and {TT}\{TT\}. This calculation also appears in the interpretations deck. Mutual exclusivity is a requirement on the sample space; it says nothing about the probabilities assigned to its elements, and counting the members is valid only when they happen to be equally probable.


The same reading in the Bertrand construction
The sampling procedures in Section 3 produce a geometric chord almost surely. After excluding the stated null cases, we may describe their outputs on the common space 𝒞*\mathcal C_* of nondegenerate, nondiameter chords. In this output description, a chord is an elementary outcome. The three rotationally invariant models use the same chord space and event collection but different probability measures. Their original sampling outcomes can instead be angles, distances or points; Section 3 distinguishes these descriptions.
The event E={c:L(c)>3R}E=\{c:L(c)>\sqrt3R\} is not an outcome. It is a set containing uncountably many chords, and it is assigned a probability as a set.
This last point also marks the limit of the summation rule above. In a continuous model each individual outcome has probability zero, so
∑c∈EP({c})=0≠P(E),\sum_{c\in E}P(\{c\})=0\ne P(E),
and the probability of EE cannot be recovered by adding the probabilities of the outcomes it contains. Countable additivity is additivity over countably many disjoint events, and EE is not a countable union of its singletons. The rule P(A)=∑ω∈AP({ω})P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\}) applies to countable events with measurable singletons; it does not extend to an uncountable event by countable additivity.


Event collections and the probability triplet
The main notes use all subsets as events for finite experiments. Here are the precise requirements for a general triplet (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P).






NoteDefinitions: power set and sigma-algebra



The power set 𝒫(Ω)=2Ω={E:E⊆Ω}\mathcal P(\Omega)=2^\Omega=\{E:E\subseteq\Omega\} contains every subset, including ⌀\varnothing and Ω\Omega. For finite |Ω|=n|\Omega|=n, it has 2n2^n elements, since including or excluding each outcome gives two choices. An event collection ℱ\mathcal F is a subset of 𝒫(Ω)\mathcal P(\Omega), so its members are themselves subsets of Ω\Omega.
The event collection ℱ\mathcal F must be a sigma-algebra on Ω\Omega. Its requirements are:

Contains the sample space: Ω∈ℱ\Omega\in\mathcal F.
Closed under complements: if E∈ℱE\in\mathcal F, then Ec=Ω\E∈ℱE^c=\Omega\setminus E\in\mathcal F.
Closed under countable unions: if E1,E2,…∈ℱE_1,E_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F, then ⋃i=1∞Ei∈ℱ\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}E_i\in\mathcal F.

These conditions ensure that “not EE” and “at least one of E1,E2,…E_1,E_2,\ldots” are events whenever the component sets are events. Since this example has a finite sample space, taking ℱ=2Ω\mathcal F=2^\Omega, the power set, satisfies all three requirements.
No disjointness assumption is needed for closure under unions. It is needed when applying countable additivity of probability. Closure also gives ⌀∈ℱ\varnothing\in\mathcal F, countable intersections by De Morgan’s law, and differences E\F=E∩FcE\setminus F=E\cap F^c.








NoteThe three probability axioms



For events in ℱ\mathcal F:
P(E)≥0,P(Ω)=1,P(E)\ge0,\qquad P(\Omega)=1,
and, for pairwise disjoint E1,E2,…E_1,E_2,\ldots,
P(⋃n=1∞En)=∑n=1∞P(En).P\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\right)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(E_n).
Pairwise disjoint means Ei∩Ej=⌀E_i\cap E_j=\varnothing for i≠ji\ne j. This assumption is needed to add probabilities without double-counting; it is not needed for sigma-algebra closure under unions.


Two familiar properties follow rather than being separate axioms. Additivity for Ω\Omega and ⌀\varnothing gives 1=1+P(⌀)1=1+P(\varnothing), hence P(⌀)=0P(\varnothing)=0. Additivity for EE and EcE^c gives
P(E)+P(Ec)=1.P(E)+P(E^c)=1.
Nonnegativity then gives P(E)≤1P(E)\le1. More generally, inclusion E⊆FE\subseteq F implies P(E)≤P(F)P(E)\le P(F) by splitting FF into EE and F\EF\setminus E.
The axioms do not impose uniformity. On a finite space, any nonnegative singleton weights summing to 1 define a probability measure on the full power set by addition.


Worked example: a die observed through two LEDs
Roll a stipulated fair six-sided die, but suppose a sensor displays only two binary readings. The red LED lights for
A={1,2},A=\{1,2\},
and the green LED lights for
B={2,3,4}.B=\{2,3,4\}.
Let X=𝟏AX=\mathbf1_A and Y=𝟏BY=\mathbf1_B: each indicator is 1 when its event occurs and 0 otherwise.

Red X(ω)X(\omega)
Green Y(ω)Y(\omega)

What can we determine from the sensor? Both LEDs identify outcome 2. Green alone identifies the group {3,4}\{3,4\}, but not the individual face. In particular, outcome 3 lights only the green LED.
The four distinguishable groups are
C10={1},C11={2},C01={3,4},C00={5,6}.C_{10}=\{1\},\quad C_{11}=\{2\},\quad
C_{01}=\{3,4\},\quad C_{00}=\{5,6\}.
Under the fair-die assumption, their probabilities are 1/6,1/6,1/3,1/31/6,1/6,1/3,1/3 respectively. They are disjoint, cover the six outcomes, and have probabilities summing to 1.
The events AA and BB are not complements. They overlap at outcome 2, and their union omits outcomes 5 and 6:
A∩B={2},A∪B={1,2,3,4}.A\cap B=\{2\},\qquad A\cup B=\{1,2,3,4\}.
Thus
P(A∪B)=26+36−16=46.P(A\cup B)=\frac26+\frac36-\frac16=\frac46.
This calculation motivates the distinction between the selected die face, an event containing several faces, and the information available from the readings.


The sensor sigma-algebra and the full model
Every event decidable from the LED pair must include or exclude an entire indistinguishable group. If it included 3 but excluded 4, the green-only reading would not determine whether that event occurred.
Consequently the sensor collection consists of all unions of
{1},{2},{3,4},{5,6}.\{1\},\quad\{2\},\quad\{3,4\},\quad\{5,6\}.
These groups are the atoms of this finite event collection: its nonempty events that cannot be split into smaller nonempty events within the collection. They are not necessarily individual outcomes.
Write
𝒢=σ(X,Y)=σ(A,B)={⋃C∈𝒥C:𝒥⊆{C10,C11,C01,C00}}.\mathcal G=\sigma(X,Y)=\sigma(A,B)
=\left\{\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal J}C:
\mathcal J\subseteq\{C_{10},C_{11},C_{01},C_{00}\}\right\}.
The empty choice gives ⌀\varnothing, and choosing all four gives Ω\Omega. There are 24=162^4=16 distinct events. Complements select the remaining atoms; unions select any atom appearing in a constituent event. These operations stay within the collection, including countable unions, so 𝒢\mathcal G is a sigma-algebra.
The notation σ(A,B)\sigma(A,B) means the smallest sigma-algebra containing AA and BB. It must contain their four intersections with complements,
A∩Bc,A∩B,Ac∩B,Ac∩Bc,A\cap B^c,\quad A\cap B,\quad A^c\cap B,\quad A^c\cap B^c,
which are precisely the four atoms above. It therefore contains all their unions. Conversely, that collection of unions is already a sigma-algebra containing AA and BB, establishing that it is the smallest one.

Is {3}\{3\} impossible, or does its probability fail to exist?
Neither follows from the sensor restriction. Keep the two models explicit:








Model
Event collection
Does it assign a probability to {3}\{3\}?




Full fair-die model (Ω,𝒫(Ω),P)(\Omega,\mathcal P(\Omega),P)
All 64 subsets
Yes: P({3})=1/6P(\{3\})=1/6


Sensor model (Ω,𝒢,P|𝒢)(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})

Here P|𝒢P|_{\mathcal G} is the restriction of the original measure: retain its values only for events in 𝒢\mathcal G. It assigns
P|𝒢({3,4})=13,P|_{\mathcal G}(\{3,4\})=\frac13,
but P|𝒢({3})P|_{\mathcal G}(\{3\}) is undefined because {3}\{3\} is outside its domain. It is not zero.
The fair-die model still permits inference about the hidden face. For instance, it gives
P({3}∣{3,4})=1/61/3=12.P(\{3\}\mid\{3,4\})=\frac{1/6}{1/3}=\frac12.
This inference uses the full model and its fairness assumption. It does not mean that the sensor can identify whether 3 occurred.


The observation does not determine a hidden probability split
Even knowing the probabilities of all four sensor readings does not identify how their masses are divided within {3,4}\{3,4\} or {5,6}\{5,6\}. For example, these two full-space assignments agree on every event in 𝒢\mathcal G:

They both give green-only probability 1/31/3, yet disagree on {3}\{3\}. The alternative is not fair; it demonstrates what the sensor-reading distribution alone cannot establish. Fairness is additional model information.






NoteMeasurability versus observability



In general, a sigma-algebra specifies the domain of a probability measure. It need not come from a physical sensor. When it is generated by observations, it describes event statements decidable from those observations. An event can be measurable in a fuller model while being indistinguishable using a particular sensor. Neither exclusion from a smaller sigma-algebra nor probability zero should be confused with logical impossibility.





A continuous triplet on the unit interval
Suppose a simulation selects a number uniformly from the unit interval. What is the probability that the selected value lies between 1/41/4 and 3/43/4? Uniformity means that an interval’s probability is its length, so the answer should be 3/4−1/4=1/23/4-1/4=1/2. To make this a probability model, we must specify more than intervals: “outside this interval” and “in at least one of these intervals” must also be events.
Take Ωu=[0,1]\Omega_u=[0,1]. A sample point u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] is a number; an event is a suitable set of numbers. We use the Borel σ-algebra
ℱu=ℬ([0,1])=σ({(a,b)∩[0,1]:a,b∈ℝ,a<b}).\mathcal F_u=\mathcal B([0,1])
=\sigma\bigl(\{(a,b)\cap[0,1]:a,b\in\mathbb R,\ a<b\}\bigr).
Here σ(𝒜)\sigma(\mathcal A) means the smallest σ-algebra containing every member of a family 𝒜\mathcal A. Equivalently, it is the intersection of all σ-algebras on [0,1][0,1] that contain that family. Such σ-algebras exist because the power set 2[0,1]2^{[0,1]} is one of them. The intervals intersected with [0,1][0,1] generate all the relatively open sets of the unit interval.
A Borel set is one member of ℬ([0,1])\mathcal B([0,1]). The Borel σ-algebra is the collection of all those members. For example,
[1/4,3/4]∈ℬ([0,1]),[1/4,3/4]⊆[0,1].[1/4,3/4]\in\mathcal B([0,1]),\qquad [1/4,3/4]\subseteq[0,1].
The first statement says it is a measurable event; the second says its elements are possible outcomes.

What the Borel σ-algebra contains
It contains ⌀\varnothing, [0,1][0,1], every relatively open or closed subset, every interval within [0,1][0,1] (including half-open intervals), and every singleton {u}\{u\}. It is closed under complements relative to [0,1][0,1], countable unions and countable intersections. The intersection property follows from De Morgan’s law:
⋂n=1∞En=[0,1]\⋃n=1∞([0,1]\En).\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n
=[0,1]\setminus\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl([0,1]\setminus E_n\bigr).
For example, each set [0,1]∩(u−1/n,u+1/n)[0,1]\cap(u-1/n,u+1/n) is relatively open, and
{u}=⋂n=1∞([0,1]∩(u−1/n,u+1/n)).\{u\}=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl([0,1]\cap(u-1/n,u+1/n)\bigr).
Thus singletons are Borel. Every countable set of points in [0,1][0,1] is then Borel, being a countable union of singletons. In particular, ℚ∩[0,1]\mathbb Q\cap[0,1] is Borel, as is its complement, the irrational points in [0,1][0,1].
These examples do not exhaust the collection: The collection includes sets formed through repeated countable unions, intersections and complements, beyond the examples listed. Closure under countable operations does not imply closure under arbitrary uncountable unions. The Borel σ-algebra is smaller than 2[0,1]2^{[0,1]}; not every subset is Borel. Section 5 below constructs a set that is not Lebesgue measurable. Since every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable, that set is not Borel either.


Assigning probabilities and checking the triplet
Let λ\lambda be Lebesgue measure, the standard measure that assigns each interval its length, and restrict it to Borel subsets of [0,1][0,1]:
Pu(E)=λ(E),E∈ℬ([0,1]).P_u(E)=\lambda(E),\qquad E\in\mathcal B([0,1]).
No scaling is needed because λ([0,1])=1\lambda([0,1])=1. Our triplet is
([0,1],ℬ([0,1]),Pu).\bigl([0,1],\mathcal B([0,1]),P_u\bigr).
To verify it, check the event collection and the measure separately.

Event collection. Every σ-algebra in the defining intersection contains [0,1][0,1] and is closed under relative complements and countable unions. Their intersection inherits these properties, so ℬ([0,1])\mathcal B([0,1]) is a σ-algebra.
Nonnegativity. Lebesgue measure is nonnegative, so Pu(E)≥0P_u(E)\ge0 for each Borel event EE.
Normalization. Pu([0,1])=λ([0,1])=1P_u([0,1])=\lambda([0,1])=1.
Countable additivity. For pairwise disjoint Borel events E1,E2,…E_1,E_2,\ldots, the countable additivity of Lebesgue measure gives
Pu(⋃n=1∞En)=∑n=1∞Pu(En).P_u\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P_u(E_n).

Here we use the standard theorem that Lebesgue measure exists and is countably additive on Borel sets. Checking a few intervals alone would not establish that theorem. Restricting this measure to the unit interval verifies all the probability axioms, and Pu(E)≤1P_u(E)\le1 follows from E⊆[0,1]E\subseteq[0,1].

The rational points are dense in [0,1][0,1], but still have probability zero in this model. The measure is length, not the number of points or how closely they are spaced.
For an explicit countable-additivity calculation, let
In=(2−(n+1),2−n],n=0,1,2,….I_n=(2^{-(n+1)},2^{-n}],\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.
These Borel intervals are pairwise disjoint and have union (0,1](0,1]. Hence
Pu((0,1])=∑n=0∞2−(n+1)=1.P_u((0,1])=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{-(n+1)}=1.
Adding the zero-probability singleton {0}\{0\} gives Pu([0,1])=1P_u([0,1])=1. This example illustrates countable additivity. It does not license an uncountable sum of singleton probabilities.
We can also use the larger Lebesgue sigma-algebra ℒ([0,1])\mathcal L([0,1]), obtained by completing Borel length: include every subset of a Borel set of length zero. This does not include every subset of the interval. Section 5 explains the obstruction for standard length.



Why countable operations matter
On a finite space, a countable union can involve only finitely many distinct subsets. On [0,1][0,1], infinite sequences of events give genuinely new constructions. For example,
An=[0,1−1/n],n≥2,⋃n=2∞An=[0,1),A_n=[0,1-1/n],\quad n\ge2,
\qquad \bigcup_{n=2}^{\infty}A_n=[0,1),
and
Bn=[0,1/n],n≥1,⋂n=1∞Bn={0}.B_n=[0,1/n],\quad n\ge1,
\qquad \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}B_n=\{0\}.
Under uniform length, the first sequence has probabilities tending to 1, while the second has probabilities tending to 0. Countable additivity implies continuity of probability: for increasing events the probability of the union is the limit of their probabilities, and for decreasing events in a probability space the probability of the intersection is their limit. Thus the singleton {0}\{0\} has probability zero even though 0 remains a possible sample point.
This explains why closure under finite combinations alone would not suffice for the usual treatment of limiting events.

2. Random variables, inverse images and probability laws
On a probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), a real-valued random variable is a measurable function
X:Ω→ℝ.X:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R.
Measurability means that X−1(B)∈ℱX^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F for every Borel set B∈ℬ(ℝ)B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R). The Borel σ-algebra is generated by open intervals and includes the intervals, singleton sets and their countable combinations used here. For a real-valued function, it is sufficient to check {ω:X(ω)≤x}∈ℱ\{\omega:X(\omega)\le x\}\in\mathcal F for every real xx.

The distinction between a random variable and a set function
A random variable is a function on outcomes, not a real-valued set function on events. It induces the following map between collections of sets:
X−1:ℬ(ℝ)→ℱ,B↦{ω:X(ω)∈B}.X^{-1}:\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad
B\longmapsto\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\}.
The probability measure and the distribution of XX are real-valued set functions:
P:ℱ→[0,1],PX:ℬ(ℝ)→[0,1],P:\mathcal F\to[0,1],\qquad P_X:\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\to[0,1],
PX(B)=P(X−1(B))=P(X∈B).P_X(B)=P\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr)=P(X\in B).
Thus a numerical question about XX is first converted to a set of outcomes, and that event is assigned a probability. This is the set-based construction used in the Bertrand calculation below. It follows the distinction in Jagannathan, Chapter 11, Definitions 68–70.


Independence used in the examples
Events E,FE,F are independent when P(E∩F)=P(E)P(F)P(E\cap F)=P(E)P(F). Random variables U,VU,V are independent when this identity holds for the events {U∈A}\{U\in A\} and {V∈B}\{V\in B\} for every pair of Borel sets A,BA,B. For variables with a joint density on a product domain, fU,V(u,v)=fU(u)fV(v)f_{U,V}(u,v)=f_U(u)f_V(v) almost everywhere implies independence: integrating over A×BA\times B separates into the product of the two marginal integrals. Independent fair tosses below stipulate the product measure, giving each ordered pair mass (1/2)(1/2)=1/4(1/2)(1/2)=1/4.


Worked example: the head count
For two independent fair tosses, each outcome in Ω={HH,HT,TH,TT}\Omega=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\} has probability 1/41/4, and ℱ=2Ω\mathcal F=2^\Omega. Define X(HH)=2X(HH)=2, X(HT)=X(TH)=1X(HT)=X(TH)=1, and X(TT)=0X(TT)=0. Then
PX({1})=P({HT,TH})=1/2,P_X(\{1\})=P(\{HT,TH\})=1/2,
PX([1,2])=P({HH,HT,TH})=3/4.P_X([1,2])=P(\{HH,HT,TH\})=3/4.
The distribution assigns probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/41/4,1/2,1/4 to 0,1,20,1,2. It is obtained through inverse images, not by assuming that the three numerical values are equally likely.


Worked example: an indicator
For an event A∈ℱA\in\mathcal F, its indicator is the random variable
𝟏A(ω)={1,ω∈A,0,ω∉A.\mathbf1_A(\omega)=\begin{cases}1,&\omega\in A,\\0,&\omega\notin A.\end{cases}
Its inverse images satisfy 𝟏A−1({1})=A\mathbf1_A^{-1}(\{1\})=A and 𝟏A−1({0})=Ac\mathbf1_A^{-1}(\{0\})=A^c. Consequently, P(𝟏A=1)=P(A)P(\mathbf1_A=1)=P(A).
For the parity model in the event-collection lab, take 𝒢={⌀,{2,4,6},{1,3,5},Ω}\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\{2,4,6\},\{1,3,5\},\Omega\}. The indicator of an even face is measurable. The numerical face-value function is not measurable relative to that σ-algebra, since the inverse image of {6}\{6\} is the unavailable subset {6}\{6\}.


Measurability and the probability law
Return to the six-ticket audit of Section 1, with B={t1,t2,t5}B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}, XB=𝟏BX_B=\mathbf1_B, and 𝒢={⌀,B,Bc,Ω}\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega\}.
To calculate P(XB∈D)P(X_B\in D), the inverse image XB−1(D)X_B^{-1}(D) must be an event. For example, XB−1((1/2,3/2))=B∈ℱX_B^{-1}((1/2,3/2))=B\in\mathcal F, giving probability 1/21/2. This requirement motivates the formal definition.
As with the unit interval in Section 1, now on ℝ\mathbb R, the Borel σ-algebra ℬ(ℝ)\mathcal B(\mathbb R) is the smallest sigma-algebra containing all open intervals. It includes intervals, singletons and their countable unions, intersections and complements. A function X:Ω→ℝX:\Omega\to\mathbb R is measurable, and hence a real-valued random variable on (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), if
X−1(D)∈ℱfor every D∈ℬ(ℝ).X^{-1}(D)\in\mathcal F\quad\text{for every }D\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).
Its law or distribution is the probability measure
PX(D)=P(X−1(D)),D∈ℬ(ℝ).P_X(D)=P(X^{-1}(D)),\qquad D\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).
In the full finite model every function is measurable because all subsets are events. For XBX_B, the inverse image is one of ⌀,B,Bc,Ω\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega according to whether DD contains neither of 0 and 1, only 1, only 0, or both. Thus XBX_B is measurable even for the smaller collection 𝒢\mathcal G. Its law assigns mass 1/21/2 each to 0 and 1. By contrast, the ID-code function J(ti)=iJ(t_i)=i is not measurable for 𝒢\mathcal G: J−1({1})={t1}J^{-1}(\{1\})=\{t_1\} is unavailable in that collection. It is measurable for 2Ω2^\Omega.


What a random variable generates
The pair of LED readings separates the four groups in the LED example above. A single numerical recording similarly determines an event collection. The qualification is that it determines the smallest compatible collection, not necessarily the full collection of the model.






NotePrecise statement



Given a function X:Ω→ℝX:\Omega\to\mathbb R, with Borel sets as the events on its numerical output space, define
σ(X)={X−1(B):B∈ℬ(ℝ)}.\boxed{\sigma(X)=\{X^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}.}
Here X−1(B)={ω:X(ω)∈B}X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\} is an inverse image, not an inverse function. The collection is the smallest sigma-algebra on Ω\Omega making XX measurable.
If a probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P) is already specified, XX is a random variable on it precisely when σ(X)⊆ℱ\sigma(X)\subseteq\mathcal F. Equality is not required. Also, XX alone does not determine PP.


Why is this collection a sigma-algebra? The inverse image of ℝ\mathbb R is Ω\Omega, and inverse images preserve complements and countable unions:
X−1(Bc)=(X−1(B))c,X−1(⋃nBn)=⋃nX−1(Bn).X^{-1}(B^c)=\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr)^c,\qquad
X^{-1}\left(\bigcup_n B_n\right)=\bigcup_n X^{-1}(B_n).
Any event collection making XX measurable must contain all these inverse images, establishing minimality. In particular, we can begin with a numerical function and construct σ(X)\sigma(X); to call it a random variable on an existing model, we must check compatibility with that model’s ℱ\mathcal F.
Also distinguish σ(X)\sigma(X) from the distribution PX(B)=P(X∈B)P_X(B)=P(X\in B). The former is a collection of events on the original outcome space Ω\Omega; the latter assigns probabilities to Borel sets of numerical values in ℝ\mathbb R and depends on the chosen PP.
The generated sigma-algebra consists of the Borel-event questions answerable from observing XX. For a finite-valued function, its nonempty level sets {X=x}\{X=x\} form a partition, and σ(X)\sigma(X) consists of all unions of those level sets. That finite partition rule is what makes the following examples easy to work out.

Parity as a special case
For the indicator H=𝟏{2,4,6}H=\mathbf1_{\{2,4,6\}}, the two level sets are even and odd, so
σ(H)={⌀,{2,4,6},{1,3,5},Ω}.\sigma(H)=\{\varnothing,\{2,4,6\},\{1,3,5\},\Omega\}.
The identity function J(ω)=ωJ(\omega)=\omega instead generates the full power set. On the full fair-die model both are random variables; on the parity-only model JJ is not measurable, since J−1({3})={3}J^{-1}(\{3\})=\{3\} is not an available event. A numerical assignment becomes a random variable on a specified model only when it satisfies this measurability requirement.



Worked example: three service-response categories
Consider eight hypothetical fixed service-request IDs. For this new experiment, take Ω={r1,…,r8}\Omega=\{r_1,\ldots,r_8\}. Select one uniformly and record only its response-time category. The thresholds are stipulated for this teaching example.



Request IDs

r3,r4,r5r_3,r_4,r_5
Standard: 100–500 ms inclusive

r6,r7,r8r_6,r_7,r_8

Write the three level sets as
C0={r1,r2},C1={r3,r4,r5},C2={r6,r7,r8}.C_0=\{r_1,r_2\},\quad C_1=\{r_3,r_4,r_5\},\quad C_2=\{r_6,r_7,r_8\}.
Knowing ZZ identifies one of these groups but not an individual request within it. Each union of groups is answerable from the category. Consequently,
σ(Z)={⌀,C0,C1,C2,C0∪C1,C0∪C2,C1∪C2,Ω}.\sigma(Z)=\{\varnothing,C_0,C_1,C_2,
C_0\cup C_1,C_0\cup C_2,C_1\cup C_2,\Omega\}.
There are 23=82^3=8 events, compared with 28=2562^8=256 in the full power set of request IDs. In particular, C0C_0 and C1C_1 are not complements: C0c=C1∪C2C_0^c=C_1\cup C_2.

Two overlapping events that are not complements
Let
A={Z≤1}=C0∪C1(not slow),A=\{Z\le1\}=C_0\cup C_1\quad\text{(not slow)},
B={Z≥1}=C1∪C2(not fast).B=\{Z\ge1\}=C_1\cup C_2\quad\text{(not fast)}.
Then
A∩B=C1,A∪B=Ω,Ac=C2,Bc=C0.A\cap B=C_1,\qquad A\cup B=\Omega,\qquad
A^c=C_2,\qquad B^c=C_0.
Neither event is the other’s complement: they overlap on every standard-response request. Under uniform ID selection,
P(A)=58,P(B)=68=34,P(A∩B)=38.P(A)=\frac58,\qquad P(B)=\frac68=\frac34,
\qquad P(A\cap B)=\frac38.
The union calculation checks:
P(A∪B)=58+68−38=1.P(A\cup B)=\frac58+\frac68-\frac38=1.
The category probabilities are 1/4,3/8,3/81/4,3/8,3/8. These numbers come from the sampling rule, not from the fact that there are three categories. Under a different weighting of request IDs, the same function ZZ would generate exactly the same sigma-algebra but could have a different distribution.


Building the collection from two event questions instead
Suppose the dashboard originally answers only “not slow?” and “not fast?” The answers are the two indicators 𝟏A,𝟏B\mathbf1_A,\mathbf1_B. Together they distinguish:



Pair of indicator values

Empty: impossible under these categories



Thus
σ(A,B)=σ(𝟏A,𝟏B)=σ(Z).\sigma(A,B)=\sigma(\mathbf1_A,\mathbf1_B)=\sigma(Z).
This is a useful way to teach closure: start with two questions that overlap, identify the groups their answers distinguish, and then take all unions of those groups. Each single binary observation gives at most four events; two jointly observed indicators can retain more information.

3. Bertrand’s paradox: sampling maps and induced distributions
This section develops the Bertrand question posed in Section 3 of the main notes. What is the probability that a randomly generated chord is longer than the side of an inscribed equilateral triangle? We first calculate three answers to this same plain-English question. Only then do we use the Kolmogorov triplet to identify precisely which probability problem each calculation answers.

The paradox: one question, three answers
For the unit circle, a chord at distance rr from the centre has length
L=21−r2.L=2\sqrt{1-r^2}.
Thus L>3L>\sqrt3 exactly when r<1/2r<1/2, or equivalently when the chord intersects the interior of the concentric disk of radius 1/21/2.
Consider three plausible readings of “choose a chord at random.”

Choose its angle uniformly at a fixed endpoint. Fix a=(1,0)a=(1,0) and measure an angle θ∈(0,π)\theta\in(0,\pi) from the upward tangent towards the disk. The resulting chord has length 2sin⁡θ2\sin\,\theta. It is longer than 3\sqrt3 when π/3<θ<2π/3\pi/3<\theta<2\pi/3, an interval occupying one third of the available angular range. The answer is 1/31/3.
Choose its distance from the centre uniformly. Fix the midpoint direction and choose its distance rr uniformly between 0 and 1. Draw the chord perpendicular to that radius. The favorable distances satisfy r<1/2r<1/2, half the available range. The answer is 1/21/2.
Choose its midpoint uniformly in disk area. Draw the chord perpendicular to the radius through the chosen midpoint. It is long enough exactly when the midpoint lies inside the concentric disk of radius 1/21/2. That disk occupies one quarter of the total area. The answer is 1/41/4. The centre and boundary are zero-area exceptions handled below.

We have asked the same question in words and obtained
13,12,14.\frac13,\qquad\frac12,\qquad\frac14.
Each calculation is correct for its construction. The phrase “a random chord” leaves the sampling rule unspecified: uniform angle, distance and area are different assumptions. We now use the Kolmogorov triplet to resolve the apparent contradiction.


Making the experiments precise with the Kolmogorov triplet
A probability model is a triplet (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P): Ω\Omega specifies the outcomes, ℱ\mathcal F specifies the measurable events, and PP assigns their probabilities. We now identify these three components for each calculation. We distinguish the common geometric question from the event that represents it in each sampling space.
Experiment I: a uniform angle at a fixed endpoint. Fix the endpoint a=(1,0)a=(1,0). From the upward tangent at aa, measure θ∈(0,π)\theta\in(0,\pi) towards the interior of the disk. The ray has direction (−sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ)(-\sin\,\theta,\cos\,\theta); its second intersection with the circle defines the chord. Substituting a+ℓ(−sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ)a+\ell(-\sin\,\theta,\cos\,\theta) into the circle equation gives ℓ(ℓ−2sin⁡θ)=0\ell(\ell-2\sin\,\theta)=0, so its length is L=2sin⁡θL=2\sin\,\theta.
Choose θ\theta uniformly. The triplet and measure are
Ω1=(0,π),ℱ1=ℬ((0,π)),P1(B)=1π∫Bdθ(B∈ℱ1).\Omega_1=(0,\pi),\qquad \mathcal F_1=\mathcal B((0,\pi)),\qquad
P_1(B)=\frac1\pi\int_B d\theta\quad(B\in\mathcal F_1).
Here ℬ\mathcal B is the Borel σ-algebra, generated by the open subsets of the stated domain. The favorable event and probability are
E1=(π/3,2π/3),P1(E1)=2π/3−π/3π=13.E_1=(\pi/3,2\pi/3),\qquad P_1(E_1)=\frac{2\pi/3-\pi/3}{\pi}=\frac13.
The endpoints θ=0,π\theta=0,\pi would give zero-length chords and have been excluded. The diameter at θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2 has probability zero and will also be omitted when we introduce the common chord chart.
Experiment II: a uniform distance with a fixed direction. Choose r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) uniformly, set the midpoint to (r,0)(r,0), and draw the vertical chord through it. Specifying the midpoint direction makes the chord unique; distance alone determines only its length.
Ω2=(0,1),ℱ2=ℬ((0,1)),P2(B)=∫Bdr(B∈ℱ2).\Omega_2=(0,1),\qquad \mathcal F_2=\mathcal B((0,1)),\qquad
P_2(B)=\int_B dr\quad(B\in\mathcal F_2).
The favorable event and probability are
E2=(0,1/2),P2(E2)=∫01/2dr=12.E_2=(0,1/2),\qquad P_2(E_2)=\int_0^{1/2}dr=\frac12.
Experiment III: a uniform midpoint in area. Choose a point M=(x,y)M=(x,y) uniformly in the disk and draw the chord perpendicular to OMOM through MM. To make this construction unique and nondegenerate everywhere on its domain, exclude the centre and boundary, both of which have area zero. Put

Advanced: measures on a common chord space
The triplets above complete the resolution. The remaining calculations study sampling maps and induced measures on geometric chords. They are not needed to resolve the paradox.
We consider three rotationally invariant models independently:

Model A: choose two independent uniform endpoints on the circumference.
Model B: choose a uniform radial distance and an independent uniform midpoint direction.
Model C: choose a midpoint uniformly in disk area.

Their connection to Experiments I–III is Exercise 8. In particular, equal chord-length distributions need not mean equal measures on geometric chords. A common sample space does not require identical supports.

4. The induced law is a probability measure
Let X:(Ω,ℱ,P)→(ℝ,ℬ(ℝ))X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)) be measurable and define PX(B)=P(X−1(B))P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B)). Nonnegativity follows from that of PP, and
PX(ℝ)=P(X−1(ℝ))=P(Ω)=1.P_X(\mathbb R)=P(X^{-1}(\mathbb R))=P(\Omega)=1.
If B1,B2,…B_1,B_2,\ldots are pairwise disjoint Borel sets, their inverse images are pairwise disjoint events, and inverse images preserve their union. Therefore
PX(⋃n=1∞Bn)=P(⋃n=1∞X−1(Bn))=∑n=1∞P(X−1(Bn))=∑n=1∞PX(Bn).P_X\!\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}B_n\right)
=P\!\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}X^{-1}(B_n)\right)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(X^{-1}(B_n))
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P_X(B_n).
This proves that PXP_X is a probability measure. The same proof applies to the sampling maps Ψj\Psi_j and the induced measures PjP_j on the chord space. Injectivity is unnecessary for this construction: inverse images exist for all functions.

Distinct meanings of the notation f−1f^{-1}
When f:𝖲→𝖸f:\mathsf S\to\mathsf Y is a bijection, f−1(y)f^{-1}(y) denotes an element of 𝖲\mathsf S, the value of the inverse function at yy. For any subset B⊆𝖸B\subseteq\mathsf Y, the notation f−1(B)f^{-1}(B) denotes a subset of 𝖲\mathsf S, the inverse image. The latter is defined even when ff is not one-to-one. In the Bertrand construction, CC and each Ψj\Psi_j are bijections on the stated restricted domains, whereas the chord-length function LL is not one-to-one.

5. Why ordinary length cannot measure every subset
The desired length assignment is more specific than an arbitrary probability measure. It is nonnegative, countably additive, assigns an interval its ordinary length, and is unchanged by translating a measurable set along the real line.






NoteScope of the claim



The claim is not that no probability measure can exist on the power set of [0,1][0,1]. A point-mass probability, for example, can be defined on every subset. The obstruction concerns extending ordinary length to every subset while retaining countable additivity and translation invariance.



Step 1: group points that differ by a rational number
For x,y∈[0,1]x,y\in[0,1], define
x∼y⇔x−y∈ℚ.x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Q.
For example, 0.10.1 and 0.30.3 belong to the same group because their difference is rational. The points 00 and 2/2\sqrt2/2 belong to different groups.
This is an equivalence relation: the difference of a point with itself is rational, reversing a rational difference keeps it rational, and adding two rational differences keeps it rational. Its equivalence classes partition [0,1][0,1].


Step 2: select one representative from each group
Using the axiom of choice, choose exactly one point from each equivalence class. Let V⊆[0,1]V\subseteq[0,1] be the set of chosen representatives. Such a selection is called a Vitali set here.
This is an existence construction. It does not provide an explicit list of the selected points or a simple interval description. We should not present it as a set that students can enumerate or draw accurately. The argument works for any such choice of representatives.


Step 3: examine its rational translates
For every q∈ℚ∩[−1,1]q\in\mathbb Q\cap[-1,1], define
V+q={v+q:v∈V},W=⋃q∈ℚ∩[−1,1](V+q).V+q=\{v+q:v\in V\},\qquad
W=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q\cap[-1,1]}(V+q).
There are countably infinitely many rational shifts in this range. Two facts matter.
Different translates are disjoint. If v1+q1=v2+q2v_1+q_1=v_2+q_2, then v1−v2=q2−q1v_1-v_2=q_2-q_1 is rational. Thus v1,v2v_1,v_2 belong to the same equivalence class. Because VV chose only one representative from each class, v1=v2v_1=v_2, and then q1=q2q_1=q_2.
Their union covers the unit interval but stays in a bounded interval. Every x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1] has a representative v∈Vv\in V in its class, and q=x−v∈ℚ∩[−1,1]q=x-v\in\mathbb Q\cap[-1,1]. Hence x∈V+qx\in V+q. Also 0≤v≤10\le v\le1 and −1≤q≤1-1\le q\le1 imply −1≤v+q≤2-1\le v+q\le2. Therefore
[0,1]⊆W⊆[−1,2].[0,1]\subseteq W\subseteq[-1,2].


Step 4: suppose ordinary length could measure VV
This step uses length λ\lambda on the real line as an auxiliary tool. We are not treating points outside [0,1][0,1] as outcomes of the original probability experiment.
If VV were Lebesgue measurable, its translates and their countable union would also be measurable. Put c=λ(V)c=\lambda(V). Translation invariance gives λ(V+q)=c\lambda(V+q)=c for every shift. Countable additivity and the preceding inclusions would then require
1≤λ(W)=∑q∈ℚ∩[−1,1]c≤3.1\le\lambda(W)=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q\cap[-1,1]}c\le3.
There is no nonnegative value of cc satisfying this:

If c=0c=0, the countable sum is zero, contradicting the lower bound 1.
If c>0c>0, the sum is infinite, contradicting the upper bound 3.

Thus VV is not Lebesgue measurable, and so it is not Borel either. There is no ordinary length λ(V)\lambda(V) to use as its uniform probability.
The conclusion is about the entire consistent length assignment, including the translated sets and countable unions. It is not a claim that merely writing an arbitrary number next to VV immediately contradicts the probability axioms. That number would not by itself supply the usual translation-invariant length model.


Interpretation of the construction
For finite Ω\Omega, we can assign weights to individual outcomes and add them over every subset. On [0,1][0,1], insisting on the standard uniform-length model requires an appropriate measurable event collection. The Borel or Lebesgue sigma-algebra supplies such a collection; the power set is too large for ordinary length.
This distinguishes two different reasons for excluding a set from an event collection. The finite set {1,3}\{1,3\} is omitted by a parity-only description but can be added without difficulty to the fair-die model. The Vitali set is not assigned a value by Lebesgue length even on its larger, completed sigma-algebra. Not every non-Borel set is non-Lebesgue-measurable: completion adds some non-Borel sets, but it still does not include VV.


Exact values, coarse bands and measurability
Use the uniform-length model of Section 1 and the identity random variable U(u)=uU(u)=u. Exact observation of UU gives
σ(U)=ℬ([0,1]).\sigma(U)=\mathcal B([0,1]).
If the ambient event collection is Borel, this equals ℱ\mathcal F. If the ambient model uses the completed Lebesgue collection, then σ(U)\sigma(U) is the Borel subcollection of that larger ℱ\mathcal F. Generated sigma-algebras are not automatically completed.
Now record only a band:
Z(u)={0,0≤u<0.2,1,0.2≤u<0.7,2,0.7≤u≤1.Z(u)=\begin{cases}
0,&0\le u<0.2,\\
1,&0.2\le u<0.7,\\
2,&0.7\le u\le1.
\end{cases}
Its three level sets I0,I1,I2I_0,I_1,I_2 are the displayed intervals. The generated sigma-algebra again consists of their eight possible unions. Under uniform length,
P(Z=0)=0.2,P(Z=1)=0.5,P(Z=2)=0.3.P(Z=0)=0.2,\qquad P(Z=1)=0.5,\qquad P(Z=2)=0.3.
For the overlapping questions A={Z≤1}A=\{Z\le1\} and B={Z≥1}B=\{Z\ge1\},
P(A)=0.7,P(B)=0.8,P(A∩B)=0.5.P(A)=0.7,\qquad P(B)=0.8,\qquad P(A\cap B)=0.5.
The event [0,0.1][0,0.1] is Borel in the full model, but does not belong to σ(Z)\sigma(Z): it splits the first band. Observing Z=0Z=0 does not determine whether U≤0.1U\le0.1. This is an information restriction, not a failure of that interval to possess a length.
There is also a useful limit to the construction. For the Vitali set VV, the function H=𝟏VH=\mathbf1_V still generates the abstract sigma-algebra
σ(H)={⌀,V,Vc,[0,1]}.\sigma(H)=\{\varnothing,V,V^c,[0,1]\}.
However, it is not a random variable on the Borel or Lebesgue uniform-length model, because its inverse-image event VV is not in the ambient event collection. We could give the two groups an arbitrary probability assignment on this four-set collection, but that would not provide the standard uniform-length model on all ordinary intervals together with VV and its translates.


An equivalent construction on the circle
Section 1 uses Borel sets for the continuous model. Why not simply use every subset, as in the finite audit? Under the axiom of choice, the following construction shows that a normalized, countably additive, rotation-invariant probability on a circle cannot be defined on all its subsets.

The setting
Let Ω=[0,1)\Omega=[0,1) and define addition modulo 11,
x⊕y={x+y,x+y<1,x+y−1,x+y≥1,x\oplus y=\begin{cases}x+y,&x+y<1,\\x+y-1,&x+y\ge1,\end{cases}
with ⊖\ominus the corresponding subtraction. Under ⊕\oplus the set [0,1)[0,1) is an abelian group; identifying 00 with 11 makes it a circle, and x↦x⊕tx\mapsto x\oplus t is a rotation. For A⊆[0,1)A\subseteq[0,1) write A⊕t={a⊕t:a∈A}A\oplus t=\{a\oplus t:a\in A\}.
Suppose PP assigns a nonnegative real number to every subset of [0,1)[0,1) and satisfies

P([0,1))=1P([0,1))=1;
countable additivity;
rotation invariance: P(A⊕t)=P(A)P(A\oplus t)=P(A) for all AA and all t∈[0,1)t\in[0,1).



The construction
Let ℚ0=ℚ∩[0,1)\mathbb Q_0=\mathbb Q\cap[0,1), a countable subgroup of ([0,1),⊕)([0,1),\oplus). Define x∼yx\sim y when x⊖y∈ℚ0x\ominus y\in\mathbb Q_0. This is an equivalence relation, and its classes are the cosets x⊕ℚ0x\oplus\mathbb Q_0.
By the axiom of choice, let V⊆[0,1)V\subseteq[0,1) contain exactly one element of each class.
Claim 1: the sets V⊕qV\oplus q, for q∈ℚ0q\in\mathbb Q_0, are pairwise disjoint. Suppose v1⊕q1=v2⊕q2v_1\oplus q_1=v_2\oplus q_2 with v1,v2∈Vv_1,v_2\in V. Then v1⊖v2=q2⊖q1∈ℚ0v_1\ominus v_2=q_2\ominus q_1\in\mathbb Q_0, so v1∼v2v_1\sim v_2. Since VV has one element per class, v1=v2v_1=v_2, and therefore q1=q2q_1=q_2.
Claim 2: these sets cover [0,1)[0,1). Given x∈[0,1)x\in[0,1), let v∈Vv\in V be the representative of the class of xx. Then q=x⊖v∈ℚ0q=x\ominus v\in\mathbb Q_0 and x=v⊕q∈V⊕qx=v\oplus q\in V\oplus q.
So [0,1)[0,1) is the union of countably many pairwise disjoint sets, each a rotation of VV.


The contradiction
Write c=P(V)c=P(V). Rotation invariance gives P(V⊕q)=cP(V\oplus q)=c for every qq, and countable additivity applied to the countable disjoint family of Claim 1, whose union is [0,1)[0,1) by Claim 2, gives
1=P([0,1))=∑q∈ℚ0P(V⊕q)=∑q∈ℚ0c.1=P([0,1))=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q_0}P(V\oplus q)=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q_0}c .
Since PP is nonnegative, c≥0c\ge0. If c=0c=0 the right-hand side is 00; if c>0c>0 the sum diverges. Neither equals 11, so no such PP exists.
Moreover, if VV were Lebesgue measurable, each V⊕qV\oplus q would be measurable with the same Lebesgue measure: addition modulo 1 is an ordinary translation on each of two pieces. The same countable sum would then contradict the Lebesgue measure of [0,1)[0,1) being 1. Thus VV is not Lebesgue measurable. This is the Vitali construction on the circle.


Scope of the conclusion
The contradiction uses both countable additivity and rotation invariance. Finite additivity alone does not justify the countably infinite sum above. Removing invariance changes the question: for example, the point mass P(A)=𝟏{0∈A}P(A)=\mathbf1_{\{0\in A\}} is a countably additive probability on every subset of [0,1)[0,1), but it is not rotation invariant.
The selection of VV uses the axiom of choice; the argument does not give a membership rule for VV. No restriction proved here prevents assigning probabilities to the Borel events used in this course. Intervals, disks, angular sectors and the sampling-map preimages in Section 3 are measurable. The construction explains a boundary of the all-subsets approach; it is not needed to carry out the practical calculations in the main lesson.

text:
Advanced: a continuous ticket-closure model
The triplet is often not written out in routine probability calculations. To see what remains implicit, consider a ticket selected from a specified service process, and let TcT_c be its closure time, measured in hours. The question

What is the probability that this ticket takes more than one day to close?

is written P(Tc>24)P(T_c>24), since one day is 24 hours. In an underlying ticket-system experiment, each outcome ω\omega determines a closure time Tc(ω)T_c(\omega) in hours. The event of interest is the inverse image
Tc−1((24,∞))={ω∈Ω:Tc(ω)>24}.T_c^{-1}((24,\infty))=\{\omega\in\Omega:T_c(\omega)>24\}.
For an illustrative calculation, suppose the closure time follows a Gamma distribution with shape α=2\alpha=2 and scale θ=12\theta=12 hours. These are hypothetical model parameters, not estimates from the six-ticket audit. Under the shape-scale parameterization, the density is
fTc(t)=tα−1e−t/θΓ(α)θα,t≥0.f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t/\theta}}
{\Gamma(\alpha)\theta^\alpha},\qquad t\geq 0.
Here α,θ>0\alpha,\theta>0 and Γ(a)=∫0∞ua−1e−udu\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}e^{-u}du for a>0a>0; in particular, Γ(2)=1\Gamma(2)=1. With α=2\alpha=2 and θ=12\theta=12 hours, this becomes
fTc(t)=t122e−t/12,t≥0,f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t}{12^2}e^{-t/12},\qquad t\geq0,
where tt is measured in hours. Here α\alpha is the shape parameter, not the mean. The mean in this shape-scale parameterization is E[Tc]=αθ=24E[T_c]=\alpha\theta=24 hours. The plotted curve shows this model and shades the area to the right of the 24-hour cutoff, which coincides with the mean.



Gamma density for ticket closure time TcT_c under the illustrative model. The vertical line marks both the mean and the 24-hour cutoff; the shaded right tail represents P(Tc>24 h)P(T_c>24\text{ h}).


For the six-ticket experiment in the main notes, probabilities were calculated by counting equally likely IDs: P(C)=|C|/6P(C)=|C|/6. A continuous ticket time cannot be handled by counting individual possible durations. Under a density model, the probability of an interval is the area under the density over that interval. A density value is not itself a probability; integration accumulates the density across the range. In the audit model, the corresponding finite calculation is a sum of singleton probabilities; for example, P(C)=∑ti∈CP({ti})=4/6P(C)=\sum_{t_i\in C}P(\{t_i\})=4/6. The closure-time probability is the integral of its density over the event. With the substitution u=t/12u=t/12,
P(Tc>24)=∫24∞t144e−t/12dt=∫2∞ue−udu=[−(u+1)e−u]2∞=(2+1)e−2=3e−2≈0.406.\begin{aligned}
P(T_c>24)
&=\int_{24}^{\infty}\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12}\,dt\\
&=\int_{2}^{\infty}u e^{-u}\,du\\
&=\left[-(u+1)e^{-u}\right]_2^\infty\\
&=(2+1)e^{-2}=3e^{-2}\approx0.406.
\end{aligned}
Thus, under this stipulated model, the probability that closure takes more than 24 hours is about 0.4060.406. A different shape, scale or target ticket population would give a different value. Specifying the Gamma family alone would not suffice; the parameters and their parameterization are needed.

What a probability density specifies
The calculation above uses an area, not a density height. Formally, a random variable TT has a probability density function ff if ff is nonnegative and measurable, ∫ℝf(t)dt=1\int_{\mathbb R}f(t)\,dt=1, and
P(T∈D)=∫Df(t)dtfor every Borel set D.P(T\in D)=\int_D f(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every Borel set }D.
Here f(t)=0f(t)=0 for t<0t<0. The same substitution checks normalization: ∫0∞(t/144)e−t/12dt=∫0∞ue−udu=1\int_0^\infty (t/144)e^{-t/12}dt=\int_0^\infty ue^{-u}du=1. A singleton has zero area, so P(Tc=24)=0P(T_c=24)=0, while a range can have positive probability. Not every random variable has a density; the Billing indicator has a discrete law.


The triplet for the closure-time model
For this calculation, use the following canonical probability space, which models closure time alone:
(Ωc,ℱc,Pc).(\Omega_c,\mathcal F_c,P_c).
In the calculation above, the shorthand P(Tc>24)P(T_c>24) denotes Pc(Tc>24)P_c(T_c>24) on this space. It is distinct from PP, the uniform measure used for selecting one of the six audited ticket IDs.

Sample space: Ωc=[0,∞)\Omega_c=[0,\infty), the possible closure durations measured in hours.
Event collection: ℱc=ℬ([0,∞))\mathcal F_c=\mathcal B([0,\infty)), the Borel subsets of the nonnegative real line: sets obtained by intersecting Borel subsets of ℝ\mathbb R with [0,∞)[0,\infty).
Probability measure: for every E∈ℱcE\in\mathcal F_c,
Pc(E)=∫EfTc(t)dt,fTc(t)=t144e−t/12,t≥0.P_c(E)=\int_E f_{T_c}(t)\,dt,
\qquad f_{T_c}(t)=\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12},\quad t\geq0.

The density integrates to one, so Pc(Ωc)=1P_c(\Omega_c)=1. Define the random variable by Tc:Ωc→[0,∞)T_c:\Omega_c\to[0,\infty), Tc(t)=tT_c(t)=t. Thus the event of closure after 24 hours is
Tc−1((24,∞))=(24,∞)∈ℱc,T_c^{-1}((24,\infty))=(24,\infty)\in\mathcal F_c,
and its probability is
Pc(Tc>24)=Pc((24,∞))=∫24∞fTc(t)dt.P_c(T_c>24)=P_c((24,\infty))
=\int_{24}^{\infty}f_{T_c}(t)\,dt.
This is one explicit probability space realizing the assumed Gamma law. A full ticket-system model could use outcomes that also include ticket type, priority and other information, with closure time as a function on that larger space. In routine calculations, Tc∼Gamma⁡(shape 2,scale 12 h)T_c\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\text{shape }2,\text{scale }12\text{ h}) states the induced law needed for probabilities about closure time without writing the whole triplet. The distribution of TcT_c does not by itself describe every other random quantity in the ticket system.
This is why many engineering and AI calculations work directly with random variables and their distributions after the probability-space foundation has been established.

title: 01.2 supplement · Advanced distribution theory
text:
1. Laws, PMFs and densities
Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu
Module 01 · Fundamentals of Probability and Random Signal Theory
Main lecture notes · Probability-space supplement · 01.3 tutorial: coins, records and ticket durations · 01.4 meeting problem
This supplement gives proofs and qualifications for the calculations in Lecture 01.2. The main notes contain the definitions needed for routine problem solving. All application models remain stipulated teaching models. Independent exercises appear without solutions.
Let (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P) be a probability space and X:Ω→ℝX:\Omega\to\mathbb R a measurable function. Its law is
PX(B)=P(X∈B),B∈ℬ(ℝ).P_X(B)=P(X\in B),\qquad B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).
If a countable set SS satisfies P(X∈S)=1P(X\in S)=1, the law is discrete. Countable additivity applied to disjoint events {X=x}\{X=x\} gives
PX(B)=∑x∈S∩BpX(x),pX(x)=P(X=x).P_X(B)=\sum_{x\in S\cap B}p_X(x),\qquad p_X(x)=P(X=x).
In particular, ∑x∈SpX(x)=1\sum_{x\in S}p_X(x)=1. The PMF can be set to zero off SS. XX may take values outside SS on a PP-null set of outcomes; the countable support describes where the law places mass.
A law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure if it admits a measurable nonnegative density fXf_X satisfying
PX(B)=∫BfX(x)dxfor every Borel B.P_X(B)=\int_B f_X(x)\,dx\quad\text{for every Borel }B.
It follows that ∫ℝfX=1\int_{\mathbb R}f_X=1. Densities differing only on a set of Lebesgue measure zero describe the same law. Their values at individual endpoints have no effect on probabilities.

title: 01.2 supplement · Advanced distribution theory
text:
Why “no point masses” is not the full density condition
Every law with a density has P(X=x)=0P(X=x)=0 for each xx. The converse does not hold in full generality: there are singular continuous laws with no atoms and no density with respect to length. The main lecture deliberately confines its continuous calculations to laws admitting PDFs.
A useful boundary case is a mixed law. An irrigation planner needs to distinguish a completely dry day from a day with some rain. Let RR be the daily rainfall in millimetres at a fixed field location. A zero reading represents no rain; positive amounts vary continuously in this simplified model. For a day selected under the stipulated rainfall model, let P(R=0)=0.3P(R=0)=0.3 and, given a positive amount, let RR be uniform on (0,10)(0,10) mm. Then for Borel BB,
P(R∈B)=0.3𝟏{0∈B}+0.07∫B∩(0,10)dr.P(R\in B)=0.3\,\mathbf1_{\{0\in B\}}
+0.07\int_{B\cap(0,10)}dr.
The continuous component integrates to 0.70.7; the remaining 0.30.3 is an atom at zero. This law cannot be represented by an ordinary PDF alone. Its CDF is
FR(r)={0,r<0,0.3+0.07r,0≤r<10,1,r≥10.F_R(r)=\begin{cases}
0,&r<0,\\
0.3+0.07r,&0\le r<10,\\
1,&r\ge10.
\end{cases}
In particular P(R>5)=0.35P(R>5)=0.35. A function that merely equals 0.070.07 on (0,10)(0,10) misses the dry-day mass.

text:
2. CDF properties and endpoints
For any real-valued random variable, FX(x)=P(X≤x)F_X(x)=P(X\le x). If a<ba<b, the disjoint decomposition
{X≤b}={X≤a}∪{a<X≤b}\{X\le b\}=\{X\le a\}\cup\{a<X\le b\}
gives P(a<X≤b)=FX(b)−FX(a)P(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a). Define
FX(a−)=limt↑aFX(t)=P(X<a).F_X(a^-)=\lim_{t\uparrow a}F_X(t)=P(X<a).
Then
P(a≤X≤b)=FX(b)−FX(a−),P(X=a)=FX(a)−FX(a−).P(a\le X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a^-),\qquad
P(X=a)=F_X(a)-F_X(a^-).
The continuity properties follow from continuity of probability on monotone sequences of events. For example, {X≤x+1/n}\{X\le x+1/n\} decreases to {X≤x}\{X\le x\}, so FX(x+1/n)→FX(x)F_X(x+1/n)\to F_X(x), establishing right continuity. The events {X≤n}\{X\le n\} increase to Ω\Omega, while {X≤−n}\{X\le-n\} decrease to the empty set; hence the limiting values are 1 and 0.
If a PDF exists, FX(x)=∫−∞xfX(t)dtF_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f_X(t)dt is absolutely continuous and FX′=fXF_X'=f_X almost everywhere. An arbitrary CDF need not have this property. In particular, differentiating the rainfall CDF away from zero cannot recover its atom.

title: 01.2 supplement · Advanced distribution theory
text:
3. Marginalization and normalization
Let X,YX,Y be discrete on countable sets SX,SYS_X,S_Y. For fixed xx, the events {X=x,Y=y}\{X=x,Y=y\}, as yy varies, are disjoint and their union agrees with {X=x}\{X=x\} up to a null event. Thus
pX(x)=∑y∈SYpX,Y(x,y).p_X(x)=\sum_{y\in S_Y}p_{X,Y}(x,y).
Summing in xx gives ∑xpX(x)=1\sum_xp_X(x)=1. Nonnegative series may be summed in either order. The corresponding proof applies to pYp_Y.
For a jointly absolutely continuous pair with density fX,Yf_{X,Y}, define
g(x)=∫ℝfX,Y(x,y)dy.g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy.
Tonelli’s theorem permits the iterated integral because the integrand is measurable and nonnegative. For Borel BB,
P(X∈B)=∬B×ℝfX,Y(x,y)dxdy=∫Bg(x)dx.P(X\in B)=\iint_{B\times\mathbb R}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy
=\int_B g(x)\,dx.
Therefore gg is a version of the marginal density fXf_X, and ∫g=1\int g=1. A density may be infinite on a null set, but is finite almost everywhere when its integral is 1. These exceptional values can be redefined without changing the law.
The support bounds must be retained. For the main lecture’s maintenance model, integrating over 0<y<x<10<y<x<1 gives fX(x)=2xf_X(x)=2x on (0,1)(0,1) and fY(y)=2(1−y)f_Y(y)=2(1-y) on (0,1)(0,1), both zero elsewhere. Extending the density value 2 across the whole unit square would double its total mass.

title: 01.2 supplement · Advanced distribution theory
text:
4. Conditional distributions and their scope

Discrete conditioning
For pX(x)>0p_X(x)>0,
pY∣X(y∣x)=pX,Y(x,y)pX(x).p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}.
Nonnegativity is inherited from the joint PMF, and
∑ypY∣X(y∣x)=∑ypX,Y(x,y)pX(x)=1.\sum_y p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)
=\frac{\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}=1.
Multiplying by pX(x)p_X(x) and summing over positive-mass xx gives the law of total probability:
pY(y)=∑x:pX(x)>0pY∣X(y∣x)pX(x).p_Y(y)=\sum_{x:p_X(x)>0}p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x).
When pX(x)=0p_X(x)=0, the ratio is undefined. Assignments of a conditional distribution at those values do not affect the joint law or any of the resulting unconditional probabilities.


Conditioning with a joint density
For 0<fX(x)<∞0<f_X(x)<\infty, set
fY∣X(y∣x)=fX,Y(x,y)fX(x).f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}.
For almost every such xx, this is a probability density in yy. It reconstructs joint probabilities through
P(X∈B,Y∈C)=∫B(∫CfY∣X(y∣x)dy)fX(x)dx.P(X\in B,Y\in C)
=\int_B\left(\int_C f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\,dy\right)f_X(x)\,dx.
This identity is a precise way to characterize a conditional-density version. Values on an XX-null set can be changed without changing the identity. Consequently the law alone does not uniquely prescribe conditional distributions at every individual continuous conditioning value. Smooth textbook formulas choose a natural version.
For a fixed Borel set CC, let gC(u)=∫CfX,Y(u,y)dyg_C(u)=\int_C f_{X,Y}(u,y)dy. If gCg_C and fXf_X are continuous at xx and fX(x)>0f_X(x)>0, then
P(Y∈C∣x−ϵ<X<x+ϵ)=∫x−ϵx+ϵgC(u)du∫x−ϵx+ϵfX(u)du→gC(x)fX(x)=∫CfY∣X(y∣x)dy.\begin{aligned}
P(Y\in C\mid x-\epsilon<X<x+\epsilon)
&=\frac{\int_{x-\epsilon}^{x+\epsilon}g_C(u)du}
{\int_{x-\epsilon}^{x+\epsilon}f_X(u)du}\\
&\longrightarrow\frac{g_C(x)}{f_X(x)}
=\int_C f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)dy.
\end{aligned}
Divide numerator and denominator by 2ϵ2\epsilon and use continuity to justify the limit. This supports the narrow-band interpretation used for the maintenance model at interior durations. It does not divide an event probability by P(X=x)P(X=x).
For a band BB with P(X∈B)>0P(X\in B)>0, an unambiguous conditional density of YY is
fY∣X∈B(y)=∫BfX,Y(x,y)dxP(X∈B).f_{Y\mid X\in B}(y)=
\frac{\int_B f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx}{P(X\in B)}.
This averages over the selected durations with their appropriate weights; it is generally not the conditional density at the band’s midpoint. In the uniform triangular model, the probability of Y<cY<c given a<X<ba<X<b does coincide with the midpoint-conditioned probability when 0<c≤a<b<10<c\le a<b<1. That coincidence for these thresholds does not make the two conditional distributions identical.

title: 01.2 supplement · Advanced distribution theory
text:
5. Independence and factorization
Random variables X,YX,Y are independent if
P(X∈B,Y∈C)=P(X∈B)P(Y∈C)P(X\in B,Y\in C)=P(X\in B)P(Y\in C)
for every pair of Borel sets B,CB,C. In the discrete case, applying this to singleton sets gives the PMF factorization. Conversely, summing a factorized PMF over B×CB\times C proves the definition.
For a pair with a joint density, independence is equivalent to fX,Y=fXfYf_{X,Y}=f_Xf_Y almost everywhere. For the sufficient direction, integrate the product over B×CB\times C and separate the integrals. For the necessary direction, independence makes the joint law the product of the marginal laws, which has density fXfYf_Xf_Y; uniqueness of a density up to null sets gives the result.
A single unequal cell proves dependence in a discrete table. For densities, a discrepancy at one isolated point proves nothing because density values can be changed on null sets. In the maintenance example the discrepancy occupies a rectangle of positive area, so the argument in the main notes establishes dependence.

Continuous marginals need not imply a joint PDF
Suppose a data logger stores a normalized sensor reading UU and a second field VV that is an exact copy of the same reading. This is one measurement stored twice, not two separate sensor measurements. Stipulate that UU is uniform on (0,1)(0,1) and put V=UV=U. Both marginals have uniform densities, but the pair lies on the diagonal v=uv=u with probability 1. That diagonal has plane area zero, so no ordinary two-dimensional PDF can represent this joint law. The main lecture’s joint-PDF formulas assume that a joint density exists, not merely that each marginal has one.
