Gap transformations for the meeting problem
The 01.4 worked example uses the gap D=|TA−TB|D=|T_A-T_B|. Suppose TA,TBT_A,T_B are independent, identically distributed on [0,1][0,1], with density hh, extended by zero outside that interval. Their joint density is h(a)h(b)h(a)h(b).
For Z=TB−TAZ=T_B-T_A, use the transformation (a,b)↦(a,z)(a,b)\mapsto(a,z) with b=a+zb=a+z and absolute Jacobian determinant 1. Integrating out aa gives a density version
fZ(z)=∫ℝh(a)h(a+z)da.f_Z(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}h(a)h(a+z)\,da.
Identical marginals and independence make this density symmetric. For 0<d<10<d<1, folding the positive and negative gaps gives
fD(d)=fZ(d)+fZ(−d)=2∫01−dh(a)h(a+d)da.f_D(d)=f_Z(d)+f_Z(-d)=2\int_0^{1-d}h(a)h(a+d)\,da.
The original joint law assigns zero mass to the diagonal, so P(D=0)=0P(D=0)=0; there is no omitted atom when folding. The density is zero off [0,1][0,1], and choices at endpoints are immaterial. With independent but different marginal densities, retain both integrals instead of doubling one. With dependence, use the actual joint density if one exists; the product formula is not justified.
For uniform marginals h(a)=1h(a)=1 on [0,1][0,1], the integral is 2(1−d)2(1-d), matching the CDF derivation in the worked example.
For h(a)=2(1−a)h(a)=2(1-a) on [0,1][0,1], put u=1−d−au=1-d-a:
fD,E(d)=8∫01−d(1−a)(1−a−d)da=8∫01−d(d+u)udu=4d(1−d)2+83(1−d)3=83−4d+43d3.\begin{aligned}
f_{D,E}(d)
&=8\int_0^{1-d}(1-a)(1-a-d)\,da\\
&=8\int_0^{1-d}(d+u)u\,du\\
&=4d(1-d)^2+\frac83(1-d)^3
=\frac83-4d+\frac43d^3.
\end{aligned}
The factored expression shows nonnegativity on (0,1)(0,1). Its integral is
[83d−2d2+13d4]01=1.\left[\frac83d-2d^2+\frac13d^4\right]_0^1=1.
Thus, on 0≤d≤10\le d\le1,
FD,E(d)=83d−2d2+13d4=1−(1−d)3(1+d3),F_{D,E}(d)=\frac83d-2d^2+\frac13d^4
=1-(1-d)^3\left(1+\frac d3\right),
with CDF 0 below 0 and 1 above 1. This is the formula used by the interactive waiting-time demonstration. It is continuous at both endpoints, gives 139/256139/256 at d=1/4d=1/4, and does not confuse the arrival density with the gap density.

title: 01.5 supplement · Expectation and moment identities
text:
1. Integrability and induced laws
Main lecture 01.5
This supplement states existence conditions and proves the identities used in the worked lecture. Its exercises are unsolved here; solutions are instructor-only.
For a measurable real-valued XX, write X+=max⁡(X,0)X^+=\max(X,0) and X−=max⁡(−X,0)X^-=\max(-X,0). Their nonnegative Lebesgue integrals are always defined in [0,∞][0,\infty]. Define E[X]=E[X+]−E[X−]E[X]=E[X^+]-E[X^-] when the two terms are not both infinite. A finite real mean requires E[|X|]<∞E[|X|]<\infty.
If PXP_X is the induced law, then E[g(X)]=∫gdPXE[g(X)]=\int g\,dP_X whenever g(X)g(X) is nonnegative or integrable. For an indicator g=𝟏Bg=\mathbf1_B, this is precisely P(X∈B)=PX(B)P(X\in B)=P_X(B). Extend by finite linear combinations to nonnegative simple functions, then by monotone convergence to nonnegative measurable functions. Subtract positive and negative parts for integrable functions. This proves the PMF/PDF formulas used in the lecture without requiring an invertible gg.
For a standard Cauchy density f(x)=1/[π(1+x2)]f(x)=1/[\pi(1+x^2)], the positive first-moment integral is proportional to ∫0∞x/(1+x2)dx=∞\int_0^\infty x/(1+x^2)dx=\infty, and the negative part has the same infinite magnitude. The mean is undefined. Symmetric truncated integrals vanish, but this principal-value cancellation is not expectation.

title: 01.5 supplement · Expectation and moment identities
section: 2. Variance and the best constant in squared error
text:
2. Variance and the best constant in squared error
Assume E[X2]<∞E[X^2]<\infty. Cauchy–Schwarz implies E[|X|]≤E[X2]E[|X|]\le\sqrt{E[X^2]}, so the mean exists. Expanding and using linearity,
E[(X−μ)2]=E[X2]−2μE[X]+μ2=E[X2]−μ2.E[(X-\mu)^2]=E[X^2]-2\mu E[X]+\mu^2=E[X^2]-\mu^2.
For any constant aa,
E[(X−a)2]=Var⁡(X)+(a−μ)2,E[(X-a)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(X)+(a-\mu)^2,
because the cross term contains E[X−μ]=0E[X-\mu]=0. Thus the mean minimizes expected squared error among constant predictions. This does not say the mean minimizes absolute error or other losses.
Since (X−μ)2≥0(X-\mu)^2\ge0, its expectation is zero exactly when it vanishes almost surely. Hence zero variance is equivalent to X=μX=\mu almost surely.

title: 01.5 supplement · Expectation and moment identities
text:
3. Covariance and linear combinations
For finite second moments, Cauchy–Schwarz makes E[|XY|]E[|XY|] finite. Expanding the centered product gives Cov⁡(X,Y)=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]. Bilinearity then gives
Var⁡(∑iaiXi)=∑i,jaiajCov⁡(Xi,Xj)=aTΣa.\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_i a_iX_i\right)=\sum_{i,j}a_i a_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=a^T\Sigma a.
Cauchy–Schwarz applied to centered variables gives |Cov⁡(X,Y)|≤σXσY|\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)|\le\sigma_X\sigma_Y. Correlation is defined only when both variances are positive. Equality corresponds to an almost-sure linear relation between the centered variables. Independence and integrability imply E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]; factorization of this one moment is not a converse criterion for independence.

title: 01.5 supplement · Expectation and moment identities
text:
4. Conditional expectation and total variance
For an integrable XX and a sigma-algebra 𝒢⊆ℱ\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F, E[X∣𝒢]E[X\mid\mathcal G] is a 𝒢\mathcal G-measurable integrable variable mm satisfying ∫AmdP=∫AXdP\int_A m\,dP=\int_A X\,dP for every A∈𝒢A\in\mathcal G. It is unique up to almost-sure equality. Taking A=ΩA=\Omega proves E[m]=E[X]E[m]=E[X]. Conditioning on a variable YY means conditioning on σ(Y)\sigma(Y). PMF and density calculations in the main notes produce versions of this object.
Assume E[X2]<∞E[X^2]<\infty and put m=E[X∣𝒢]m=E[X\mid\mathcal G]. Decompose
X−E[X]=(X−m)+(m−E[X]).X-E[X]=(X-m)+(m-E[X]).
The cross term has expectation zero because E[X−m∣𝒢]=0E[X-m\mid\mathcal G]=0 and m−E[X]m-E[X] is 𝒢\mathcal G-measurable. Therefore
Var⁡(X)=E[(X−m)2]+E[(m−E[X])2]=E[Var⁡(X∣𝒢)]+Var⁡(m).\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-m)^2]+E[(m-E[X])^2]
=E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)]+\operatorname{Var}(m).
The same decomposition proves the optimality of mm among square-integrable 𝒢\mathcal G-measurable predictors under squared-error loss.

title: 01.5 supplement · Expectation and moment identities
text:
5. Generating functions and their existence
For a nonnegative integer-valued NN, GN(s)=E[sN]G_N(s)=E[s^N] is defined for 0≤s≤10\le s\le1, using 00=10^0=1 in the series at zero. For 0<s<10<s<1 termwise derivatives follow from power-series theory. As s↑1s\uparrow1, monotone convergence gives GN′(1−)=E[N]G_N'(1^-)=E[N] and GN″(1−)=E[N(N−1)]G_N''(1^-)=E[N(N-1)], with infinite values allowed. Finite second moment yields
Var⁡(N)=GN″(1−)+GN′(1−)−GN′(1−)2.\operatorname{Var}(N)=G_N''(1^-)+G_N'(1^-)-G_N'(1^-)^2.
The moment generating function is MX(t)=E[etX]M_X(t)=E[e^{tX}] where finite. If finite on an open interval containing zero, differentiation under the integral gives MX(k)(0)=E[Xk]M_X^{(k)}(0)=E[X^k] and determines the law uniquely. For a Bernoulli variable, MX(t)=1−p+petM_X(t)=1-p+pe^t, giving first and second raw moments pp. Not every distribution has an MGF finite on such an interval, so one cannot use this method without its existence hypothesis.

title: 01.6 supplement · Change of variables and induced laws
text:
1. The general construction does not require a density
Main lecture 01.6
For a measurable map g:ℝm→ℝkg:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^k and random vector 𝑿\mathbf X, the law of 𝒀=g(𝑿)\mathbf Y=g(\mathbf X) is P𝒀(B)=P𝑿(g−1(B))P_{\mathbf Y}(B)=P_{\mathbf X}(g^{-1}(B)). Preimages preserve complements and countable unions, so this assignment is a probability measure on Borel sets. It remains valid for discrete, continuous, mixed and singular laws. The notation g−1(B)g^{-1}(B) means a set preimage, not necessarily a functional inverse.
If 𝑿\mathbf X has a density, integrate it over the preimage. A transformed density exists only if the new law is absolutely continuous with respect to the appropriate volume measure. For instance, (X,X)(X,X) lives on a diagonal and has no ordinary planar density even when XX has a density on the line.

title: 01.6 supplement · Change of variables and induced laws
text:
2. Change-of-variables theorem for densities
Let U,V⊆ℝmU,V\subseteq\mathbb R^m be open and let g:U→Vg:U\to V be a C1C^1 diffeomorphism. Let 𝑿\mathbf X have density ff with P(𝑿∈U)=1P(\mathbf X\in U)=1. Write h=g−1h=g^{-1}. By the multivariable integration theorem, for every Borel B⊆VB\subseteq V,
P(g(𝑿)∈B)=∫g−1(B)f(𝒙)d𝒙=∫Bf(h(𝒚))|det⁡Dh(𝒚)|d𝒚.\begin{aligned}
P(g(\mathbf X)\in B)
&=\int_{g^{-1}(B)}f(\mathbf x)d\mathbf x\\
&=\int_B f(h(\mathbf y))|\det Dh(\mathbf y)|d\mathbf y.
\end{aligned}
The integrand is therefore a density on VV, extended by zero elsewhere. Its integral is 1 by taking B=VB=V. The inverse function theorem gives Dh(g(𝒙))=[Dg(𝒙)]−1Dh(g(\mathbf x))=[Dg(\mathbf x)]^{-1}, so the inverse determinant is the reciprocal of the forward determinant in absolute value. Absolute value accounts for orientation reversal.
A null set excluded from the original support causes no loss of probability. When a transformation is one-to-one only on separate regions, partition the original support into those regions, apply the theorem on each, and add their densities on overlapping image regions. This proves the finite-branch formula. Critical sets with positive probability cannot simply be discarded.

title: 01.6 supplement · Change of variables and induced laws

3. Auxiliary-variable construction and convolution
If (X,Y)(X,Y) has density fX,Yf_{X,Y}, the linear map (x,y)↦(s,v)=(x+y,x)(x,y)\mapsto(s,v)=(x+y,x) is invertible on the plane with inverse (v,s−v)(v,s-v) and absolute inverse determinant 1. Hence fS,V(s,v)=fX,Y(v,s−v)f_{S,V}(s,v)=f_{X,Y}(v,s-v) and marginalization yields fS(s)=∫fX,Y(v,s−v)dvf_S(s)=\int f_{X,Y}(v,s-v)dv. Nonnegativity permits the iterated integral by Tonelli’s theorem. Product convolution is obtained only under independence.
For a signed difference R=Y−XR=Y-X, take V=XV=X: fR(r)=∫fX,Y(v,v+r)dvf_R(r)=\int f_{X,Y}(v,v+r)dv. Under iid densities hh, symmetry gives fR(r)=fR(−r)f_R(r)=f_R(-r); folding yields f|R|(d)=2fR(d)f_{|R|}(d)=2f_R(d) for d>0d>0, provided no atom at zero is omitted. The meeting model has none because the diagonal has probability zero.

4. Inverse-CDF generation
For a CDF FF, let Q(u)=inf⁡{x:F(x)≥u}Q(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}, 0<u<10<u<1. The CDF properties imply Q(u)≤xQ(u)\le x if and only if u≤F(x)u\le F(x). Thus if U∼U(0,1)U\sim U(0,1),
P(Q(U)≤x)=P(U≤F(x))=F(x).P(Q(U)\le x)=P(U\le F(x))=F(x).
This argument handles jumps and flat portions; ordinary functional inversion is not required. Uniform endpoint values have probability zero in the mathematical model, but implementations of logarithmic generators must avoid evaluating log⁡0\log0.

5. Polar transformation and standard-normal generation
Let U1,U2U_1,U_2 be independent uniform variables on (0,1)(0,1). Set R=−2log⁡U1R=\sqrt{-2\log U_1} and Θ=2πU2\Theta=2\pi U_2. For r≥0r\ge0, P(R≤r)=1−e−r2/2P(R\le r)=1-e^{-r^2/2}, so fR(r)=re−r2/2f_R(r)=re^{-r^2/2} for r>0r>0. The angle is uniform on (0,2π)(0,2\pi) and independent of RR.
Set Z1=Rcos⁡ΘZ_1=R\cos\Theta, Z2=Rsin⁡ΘZ_2=R\sin\Theta. Away from a null origin and angle cut, the polar-to-Cartesian absolute determinant is rr. Hence
fZ1,Z2(z1,z2)=re−r2/22π1r=12πe−(z12+z22)/2=ϕ(z1)ϕ(z2).f_{Z_1,Z_2}(z_1,z_2)=\frac{re^{-r^2/2}}{2\pi}\frac1r

title: 01.7 supplement · Gaussian structure and conditional laws
text:
1. Definition including singular laws
Main lecture 01.7
A Gaussian vector can be represented as 𝑿=𝝁+A𝒁\mathbf X=\boldsymbol\mu+A\mathbf Z for independent standard normal components of 𝒁\mathbf Z, with covariance Σ=AAT\Sigma=AA^T. The characteristic function is
φ𝑿(t)=E[eitT𝑿]=exp⁡(itT𝝁−12tTΣt).\varphi_{\mathbf X}(t)=E[e^{it^T\mathbf X}]
=\exp(it^T\boldsymbol\mu-\tfrac12t^T\Sigma t).
This follows by independence and the standard-normal characteristic function e−t2/2e^{-t^2/2}. It also shows that every linear combination is normal with its corresponding mean and variance. Conversely, the all-linear-combinations definition gives this characteristic function; uniqueness identifies the affine-normal law. A zero variance is allowed in this definition.
If Σ\Sigma is singular, there is nonzero aa with aTΣa=0a^T\Sigma a=0, so aT(𝑿−𝝁)=0a^T(\mathbf X-\boldsymbol\mu)=0 almost surely. The distribution lies in a lower-dimensional affine subspace and has no density with respect to full-dimensional Lebesgue measure. The positive-definite density formula must not be used with a zero determinant.

title: 01.7 supplement · Gaussian structure and conditional laws
section: 2. Density and normalization by an invertible map
text:
2. Density and normalization by an invertible map
For positive-definite Σ\Sigma, choose LL invertible with LLT=ΣLL^T=\Sigma, for example its Cholesky factor. The independent-standard-normal density is (2π)−p/2e−𝒛T𝒛/2(2\pi)^{-p/2}e^{-\mathbf z^T\mathbf z/2}. Under 𝒙=𝝁+L𝒛\mathbf x=\boldsymbol\mu+L\mathbf z, the inverse determinant is |det⁡L|−1=|Σ|−1/2|\det L|^{-1}=|\Sigma|^{-1/2}. Substitution gives the stated multivariate density.
Its integral is 1 because the change of variables converts it back to the product of pp normalized standard-normal densities. The covariance is LILT=ΣLIL^T=\Sigma. The factorization also proves that whitening yields independent normal coordinates; identity covariance alone would imply only uncorrelated coordinates for an arbitrary non-Gaussian vector.

title: 01.7 supplement · Gaussian structure and conditional laws
text:
3. Linear maps and marginal distributions
For a k×pk\times p matrix BB and vector bb, B𝑿+b=B𝝁+b+BA𝒁B\mathbf X+b=B\boldsymbol\mu+b+BA\mathbf Z is Gaussian with covariance BΣBTB\Sigma B^T. Taking BB to select coordinates proves the marginal property. Taking a single row proves the linear-combination property. The characteristic function above establishes that Gaussian laws are determined by their means and covariance matrices, including singular cases.

title: 01.7 supplement · Gaussian structure and conditional laws
text:
4. Conditioning in blocks
Partition the vector as (𝑿aT,𝑿bT)T(\mathbf X_a^T,\mathbf X_b^T)^T and partition 𝝁,Σ\boldsymbol\mu,\Sigma accordingly. For positive-definite Σ\Sigma, Σaa\Sigma_{aa} is invertible. Define the residual
𝑹=𝑿b−𝝁b−ΣbaΣaa−1(𝑿a−𝝁a).\mathbf R=\mathbf X_b-\boldsymbol\mu_b-\Sigma_{ba}\Sigma_{aa}^{-1}(\mathbf X_a-\boldsymbol\mu_a).
It has mean zero and cross-covariance
Cov⁡(𝑹,𝑿a)=Σba−ΣbaΣaa−1Σaa=0.\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf R,\mathbf X_a)=\Sigma_{ba}-\Sigma_{ba}\Sigma_{aa}^{-1}\Sigma_{aa}=0.
The pair (𝑹,𝑿a)(\mathbf R,\mathbf X_a) is jointly Gaussian. A block-diagonal covariance makes its characteristic function factor into the product of the two block characteristic functions, proving independence. Expansion gives
Cov⁡(𝑹)=Σbb−ΣbaΣaa−1Σab.\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf R)=\Sigma_{bb}-\Sigma_{ba}\Sigma_{aa}^{-1}\Sigma_{ab}.
Consequently a conditional-law version is
𝑿b∣𝑿a=xa∼N(𝝁b+ΣbaΣaa−1(xa−𝝁a),Σbb−ΣbaΣaa−1Σab).\mathbf X_b\mid\mathbf X_a=x_a\sim N\left(
\boldsymbol\mu_b+\Sigma_{ba}\Sigma_{aa}^{-1}(x_a-\boldsymbol\mu_a),
\Sigma_{bb}-\Sigma_{ba}\Sigma_{aa}^{-1}\Sigma_{ab}\right).
The covariance is the Schur complement and is positive definite here. The bivariate formula follows by scalar substitution. This derivation specifies a continuous density version and does not condition through a ratio with a zero-probability singleton. Conditional distributions are only uniquely determined almost everywhere in general.
The same characteristic-function factorization proves that zero cross-covariance of Gaussian subvectors is equivalent to their independence. The statement requires the joint Gaussian assumption, not merely normal marginal distributions.

title: 01.7 supplement · Gaussian structure and conditional laws
text:
5. Probability inside a bivariate ellipse
Let 𝑿∼N2(𝝁,Σ)\mathbf X\sim N_2(\boldsymbol\mu,\Sigma) with Σ\Sigma positive definite and whiten to 𝒁\mathbf Z. The squared Mahalanobis distance is
Q=(𝑿−𝝁)TΣ−1(𝑿−𝝁)=Z12+Z22.Q=(\mathbf X-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf X-\boldsymbol\mu)=Z_1^2+Z_2^2.
For c≥0c\ge0, polar integration gives
P(Q≤c)=∫02π∫0c12πe−r2/2rdrdθ=[−e−r2/2]0c=1−e−c/2.\begin{aligned}
P(Q\le c)&=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\sqrt c}\frac1{2\pi}e^{-r^2/2}r\,dr\,d\theta\\
&=\left[-e^{-r^2/2}\right]_0^{\sqrt c}=1-e^{-c/2}.
\end{aligned}
Thus QQ has a chi-square distribution with two degrees of freedom. The probability-α\alpha ellipse has c=−2log⁡(1−α)c=-2\log(1-\alpha) for 0<α<10<\alpha<1. In pp dimensions the analogous quadratic form is chi-square with pp degrees of freedom; the simple exponential CDF here is specific to p=2p=2.

text:
Further exercises
NS1. Let Σ=(4−2−24)\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}. Find its eigenvalues, principal directions and the semiaxis lengths of its 95% probability ellipse.
NS2. If 𝑿∼N2(0,Σ)\mathbf X\sim N_2(0,\Sigma) with Σ=(1114)\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}, calculate the covariance of (X1+X2,X2−X1)T(X_1+X_2,X_2-X_1)^T. Are these transformed coordinates independent?
NS3. In the same sensor model, verify total variance for X2X_2 using the conditional variance and the variance of the conditional mean.

Additional Reference
Krishna Jagannathan, Probability Foundations for Electrical Engineers, lecture notes, 9 July 2025. For 01.1, focus on Chapter 4 (§§4.1–4.5) and the elementary consequences in Chapters 5–6. Chapter 7 is optional background. The lecture notes provide an intuitive route while retaining the formal definitions.

Jay L. Devore, Probability and Statistics for Engineering and the Sciences, 8th edition: Chapter 2, §3.1 and §4.1, for probability, random variables and densities.
Alan Hájek, “Interpretations of Probability”, §§1 and 3.1–3.5, for the calculus and interpretations.
John D. Norton, “Bertrand’s Geometrical Paradoxes: Proofs”, the three chord-sampling constructions.
Richard C. Larson and Amedeo R. Odoni, Urban Operations Research, §3.3.2, comparison on common distance and angular coordinates.
Nancy Reid, Distributions for Parameters, slides 7–8 and 16, for fiducial inference and parameter distributions.
